div.head: " TOMORRA."
div.p: " TOMORRA."

IIPON". LORD TIOINYSON'S NEW IRISH POSH. An Iriqh peasant tells "his Honour" the story of Molly Magee, the poor witless one, whose answer to every greeting was "Tomorra ;" Shure, an' meself remimbers wan night comin' down:be
_ • the sthrame, Aie it seems to ma now like a bit of yesther-day in a
dhrarne-- Here where yer Honour seen her—there was but a slip
of a moon; 3tit I hard thim—Molly Magee with her batchelor—

_ _ _ Danny O'Roon- -o•You've been takin' a dhrop o' the ctathur;" an' Danny 0 says, "Troth, an' I been yer health wid Shamus O'Shea at Katty'S stiebeen; But I must be larin' ye soon." " Ochone are ye goin' away ?" "Goin' to cut. Sassenach whate," he says, "over the "An' whin will ye meet me agin ?" an' I hard :him "Molly asthore, I'll meet you agin to-morra," says he, "be the chapel. door." "An' whin are ye goin' to lave me.?" "0' Monday mornin'," says he; Aw sure thin ye'll Meet me tomorrar Tomorra, tomorra;Machree I" . _ Thin Molly's ould mother, yet Honour, thar.had no likin' for Dan, 41131 Oall'd from her cabin an' tould her to come away from the man' An' Molly Magee kern flyin' acrass me, as light as a lark, An' Dan stood,there for a minute, an' thin wint into the dark. But vrirrah the storm that night—the tundher, an' rain that fell, An' the sthrames runnin' down at the back o' the glin 'ud 'a dhrowned Hell. To-morrow comes, but Dan appears no'niore. Suitors press for the hand of fair Molly "wid the red o' the rose an' the white o' the May," but she will think of none but Dan. They try to persuade her that he has gone to America, has married another, and is lost to her; but so only waits and droops : An' either her paiirints had inter'd glory, an' both in wan day, She began to spa.ke to herself, the crathur, an' whisper, an' any "Tomorra,Tomorra!" an' Father Molowny he tuk her in
half, a Molly, you're manin', he says, "me dear, av I undher-
Stan', That yell meet your pairints agin an' yer Danny O'Roon afore God Wid his blessed Marthyrs an' Saints ;" an' she gay him a frindly nod, "Tomorra, Tomorra," she says, an' she didn't intind to
desave, But hr wits wor dead, an' her hair was as white as the

snow an a grave, At It, 40 years after, men digging the-bog came upon the body of a man, drowned in the black water. They laid it by the chapel door, and none of the parish knew who it might be:— But Molly kern limpin' up wid her stick, she was lamed
iv a kdee, Thin a slip of a gossoon call'd "Div ye know him, Molly , Magee ' An' she stood up strait as the Queen of the world--ehe
lifted her head— " He said lie would meet me tomorra!" in' dhropt down dead an the dead.

A scientist mentions a remarkable physical fact that a peach, pear, or apple always gravitates into a dealer's basket with the rosy side up. A Yankee clinched his argument with an Englishman as to the relative size of the Thames and Mississippi by saying. "Why, look here, mister, there ain't enough liater in the whole of the Thames to make a gargle for the mouth of the Mississippi river." There is an anecdote of an honest Irishman whose mingled sense of the duty of gratitude and the awk- wardness of obligation found vent in the characteristic aspiration," Oh ! that I could see your honour knocked down in a fight! Sure, and wouldn't I bring a faction to the rescue !"

Lord North, when Minister, being one day in the gang- way of one of the doors of the drawing-room at St.. James's, a lady said to him, "My lord, we want room; I wish you would get out !" "Ales, madam !" replied he, " you are not the only person who has that wish, though they do not. all tell it me to my face." . .

At a meeting of the Fife Magistrates some years after 174.5 a Whig gentleman gave as a toast "The Duke of Cumberland." David Destoun, of Kilconquhar, a zealous Jacobite, immediately after proposed "James Sibald, the butcher of Colnesburgh," to the great indignation of hia Whig neighbour, who said he must decline to do 80 much honour to a common tradesman. "Sir," said Kiicon- quhar sternly, "I've drunk your butcher, and you'll either drink mine or be put over the window." The painter, Gerard Lairesae, previous to his leaving Amsterdam, where he had made considerable fortune, had been invited to the house of an eminent painter, who requested he would favour him with one of his perform- ances. fie consented; but the painter and his pupils were greatly astonished when Lairesse, instead of draw- ing a painting, pulled from under his cloak, a violin on which he played some airs. Ile afterwards took up the pencil, sketched the subject which he proposed to execute, resumed his violin, played a few airs, then re- turned to his palette, and continued alternately playing and painting, till, in the space of three hours, L dross° had completed an exquisite painting. It was always through the assistance of his violin that this celebrated art at performed his works.

A arm; Bor's-S-se-x-ON.—Two little boys were play- ing together, and this is how they amused themselves Eddie," said Harry, "I'll be a minister and preach you :a sermon." "AU right," said Eddie, "I'll be the people." Harry began, "My text is a short and easy one—' Be kind. There are some texts in the Bible on purpose for little children, and this is one of them. There are a great many heads to my sermon. First, Be kind to pipe, and •don't make a noise when he has a headache. I don't be- lieve, Eddie, you know what a headache is; but I do. I had one once, and didn't want to hear any one speak a word; and if I heard a noise the pain was dreadful! Second, FM kind to mamma, and don't make her tell you to do a thing more than once. Think how tired she must -get saying,' It is time for you to ga to bed,' half a dozen times over. Third, Be kind to baby." "You have leaved out, be kind to Harry," interrupted Eddie. 4' Yea," said Harry, "but you will be kind to me if you are kind to all the others, because you will forget to be unkind. I was saying be kind to baby, and lend her your red soldier when she wants it. Fourth, Be kind to .Bane, and don't kick and scream when she washes you." Hem Eddie looked a little ashamed, and said, "But she pulled my hair with the comb:' "People musn't talk in meeting," said Harry. "Fifth, Be kind to kitty. Do what will make her purr, not what will make her cry." 0 Harry," cried Eddie, with tears in his eyes, "don't preach any more, 'cause I will always be kind now." IirSTAAISIBLE Doos.—Get Holland's translation of the worthy Pliny if you want an afternoon's amusement. He will tell you that, if you cut off the titfof a dog's tail within 40 days from its birth it will never go mad, and that the best of the litter is the whelp which gets its eye- sight last, or that which the mother carries first into her kennel. Of the dog's faithfulness he has notable in- stances. It has been known to throw itself into the flames when its master's funeral pyre was kindled. It -wilt breed with the tiger. The Indians cross their dogs in that way. The first and second crosses are too savage; the third can he trained. No matter haw fierce a dog is it will never attack you if you it down—Homer says the same thing in the "Odyssey,"—and it may be silenced by holding to it a brand snatched from a funeral pyre. When cremation was given up this receipt had to be modified, iind for the brand was substituted "the hand of glory,' which credulous mediceval burglars used to carry, with the view cf keeping the watchdog quiet. The most fighting breed was the Molossian, a splendid sample which the King of, Albania gave to Alexander the Great when he was going to India. Alexander had boars, stags, and bears slipped to it, but the dog lay motionless; whereat the King's anger was roused that such a noble form should cover so sluggish a spirit, and he bade the dog be killed, sending a message to the giver that the gift had proved unworthy of there both. Whereupon another like dog was sent, with the warning that the first dog's inaction in presence of small game was not due to sluggishness, but to contempt, such dogs 'being used to be matched against elephants and lions. Alexander at once tried him with a lion, which he slew, and then set him at an elephant, round which be circled, baying loudly, and with all his bristles erect, attacking first on vie side and then on the other, slipping in and avoiding the elephant's stroke whenever he got the -chance. At last the elephant grew dizzy, and, falling down, was made a prey by its small-sized antagonist.— All the Year Round.

A man must have either great men or great objects before him, otherwise his powers degenerate, as the magnet's do when it has lain a long time without being turned towards the right corners of the world. Follow with reverent steps the great example Of Him whose holy work was "doing good ;" So shall the wide earth seem our Father's temple, Each loving life a psalm of gratitude!— Whittier. Irregularity and want of method are supportable onlv in men a great learning or genius, who are often too full to be exact, and therefore choose to throw down their pearls in heaps before the. reader rather than be at the pains of stringing them. There is an Edinburgh tradition to the effect that on the occasion of a fire at a post-office, a voice was heard, with a nasal twang in it, shouting to the:firemen, "Play on the Birkintulloch bag !" The poor fellow had posted a letter-directed to that town, and it naturally was to him the supreme point of interest in the conflagration. s A traveller, recently returned from India, was relating his travelling impressions. "What a country that is !" he exclaimed. "There, everybody keeps dotens of ser- vants. I had four whose solo business it was to look after my pipe. One brought it to me, another filled it, and the third lighted it for me—." "And the fourth?" "The fourth smoked it for me. Tobacco never agreed with me." No BATHS FOR CatusrtaNs.—There is one remarkable restriction in every Persian city. No Christian is ever permitted to enter one of the public baths. These baths are on the plan of what are called the Turkish baths in Europe. The women bathe in the morning, and the men in the afternoon. After the bath the bathers lounge in an outer room and gossip and smoke. For the women especially the weekly visit to the bath is like resorting to a woman's club. They take their sewing And embroidery, and after the bath art for hours chatting, sewing, and smoking the water-pipe. When the woman returns home from the bath she is full of the gossip of the neigh- bourhood, and has plenty to talk aboutlfor a week to come. In Turkey all sects can visit the baths, but the Persians allow no one to bathe with them but the faith- ful_followers of the Prophet. . .

WAN IT Memoar you pretend to say," re- marked a lawyer to a witness, *that you remember the exact words this man said to you ton years ago?" "I do." "Well, if my memory serves me I met you at ' Saratoga about five years ago, and I should like to know if you can swear to any expression which I then made." "I can." "Now, Mr. J., I want you to remember that you are under oath. Now, under oath, you swear that you can quote with great accuracy a remark I made to you at Saratoga five years ago?' "I can." "Well, what., was it ?" "You met me in the hotel corridor." "Yes, quite correct." "And you shook kends with me." " Naturally I did." "And you said tome: 'Let's go and take someting." The crier of the court had to call ' silence for ten minutes, and the lawyer confessed that the witness had a remarkabl• smory.—Boston Journal. , How A JAPANENH GIRL 'IAMB A FALSE LOPER.— Tlle curious hold superstition has upon the minds of the I Japanese is very well- illustrated by the proceedings ' taken by a Japanese damsel when a lover proves false to his vows. When the world is at rest, at two o'clock in the morning the woman rises. She dons a white robe , and high sandals, or clogs. Her coif is a metal tripoli, in ' • which are thrust three lighted candles; around her neck , she hangs a mirror, which falls upon hor bosom; in her , left hand she carries a small straw figure—the effigy of her faithless lover—and in her right hand she grasps a hammer and nails, with .which she fastens the figure to one of the sacred trees that surround the shrine. Then she prays for the death of the traitor, vowing that if her " petition be heard she will herself pull out the nails which now offend the god by wounding the mystic tree. Night . after night she comes to the shrine, and each -night she strikes it two more nails, believing that every nail will I shorten :her lover's life; for the god,.to save his tree, will aurely strike him dead. "Keep Hee is me RITTS."—Ono of the best known residents in the town of is "Uncle Billy Smith." He is one of those jovial, genial souls, the very sight of whose face compels a smile in anticipation of the good things to come. Like many of the old schooa Uncle Billy is a thorough home lover, having rarely' been out- side his native town. A few weeks since he was visited by a 'party of nephews and nieces and beguiled into a promise to accompany thews on a fishing trip. As they were twenty miles from the beach, of course this trip Involved an early ride and the loss of the old gentleman's long-cherished morning nap.. Reaching their destination they embarked one small yarbt, and stood down the bay. It was Uncle Billy's first experience on the bounding billows, and for a time the novelty of the situation over- came all other sensations. Lan, alas! not for long. Soon abused nature, insulted by the loss of the morning's nap ;led made yet more indignant by the unaccustomed mo- tion, asserted herself. Uncle Billy collapsed on the lee rail, almost a wreck, yet still retaining sufficient life to enable him to stagger to the side of the skipper, angrily exclaiming, "Can't you keep her in the ruts? Let me drive &spell." The shout which greeted this thoroughly original idea completed Uncle Billy's discomfiture, and he went below to appear no more until the wharf was reached on the return trip.—Exchange. P,ovren OVER Axisetr.s.—The singular power some per- sons possess over animals is difficult to explain. Nearly every coentry village boasts some successful bob-taker or horse-tamer, who can manage the insects and animals in a way that his neighbours fail to do. Visitors at a dog show must have often remarked how some people get on immediately friendly terms with half the animals exhibited, fondling strange dogs with impunity, despite the warning placards above the benches. Other people are similarly fortunate with horses. Are animal's aware, 1 by a kind of intuition, that they are in the company of those who like them? or have animal-lovers some pecu- liar knack of voice and touch which gives them this power of control over the creatures? Soldiers and sailors are generally great lovers of pets, and very suc- cessful animal-tamers. Many a regiment has its favourite animal, which has accompanied the corps for years and even seen "active service." If we remember aright, a goat went with a Welsh Fusilier regiment to the'Crimers, and survived the campaign. A sailor returning. home after a cruise is tolerably certain to have a parrot or a monkey among his baggage. The Spitalfields weavers used to be great bird-fanciers, nearly every garret exhi- biting a cage or two at the window. The love of pets is an ancient and universal one, shared by king and subject, great men and obscure toilers. Walter of the Vogelweide, the celebrated thirteenth century minstrel, left a be- quest to the monks of Wurtzburg, on condition that they daily fed the birds of the air on li?s tombstone, giving as a reason for his charity that the feathered songsters had taught him the art of minstrelsy. Other poets and writers have not forgotten to acknowledge their in- debtedness to various friends in fur. and feather." ESTABLISHED NEARLY Se YEARS Vihfte'S Celebrated Moe-Hain Trusses. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 19, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. DECEMBER 19, 1885.
THE NEW PARLIAMENT.

The returns of the t eneral election are now com- plete with the exception of Orkney and Shetland, ' which were polled on Monday and Tuesday, and Edinburgh and St. Andrew's University, the polling for which took place on Wednesday and Thursday. ' The results of both these elections were expected to be declared yesterday, and in that case will be found amongst our late news. The new Parliament has now 331 Liberals, three Independent Liberals, 248 Conservatives, and 86 Nationalists. Of these 36 have been returned unopposed. In the 605 contes- ted elections, by which 631 have been returned, it is computed that 4,365,688 voters have gone to the poll, of whom 2,137,673 voted for Liberals, 1,931,601 for Conservatives, and 296,414 for Nationalists. In the boroughs of England and Wales there were 237 members returned, six being Liberals unopposed and the remaindes being returned in 209 contests, of which 22 were in double constituencies. The gross Liberal poll in 209 contests in English boroughs was 737.863; gross Conservative poll in 207 contests, 711,677. In the English counties there were 243 members returned, three of them unop- posed. The gross Liberal poll in the counties of England and Wales was 1,090,867 in 250 contests, and the Conservative poll was 958,614 in 248 con- tests. The Scotch counties returned 39 members, two being unopposed. The gross Liberal poll was 149,426 in 37 contests, and the Conservative poll 93,451 in 84 -contests. The Scotch boroughs re- turned 31 members in 27 contests, three being un- opposed. The gross number of Liberal voters in Scotch boroughs was 121,346 in the 30 contests, and the Conservatives 58,466 in `2....,‘› contests. In the Irish counties there were 85 members returned, 20' of them unopposed. The gross Liberal poll was 28,293 in 18 contests; the Conservative poll was 82,648 in 54 contests, and the Nationalists 251,257 in 58 contests. The Irish boroughs returned 16 members in 13 contests, two being unopposed. The number of Liberal votes in five contests was 7,420, •the number of Conservatives in eleven contests 26,745, and the Nationalists in ten contests 41,638. The following are the members elected : ENGLAND AND WALES.

div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.
THE EASTERN CRISIS.

REPORTED CONSPIRACY TO ASSASSINATE KING. MILAN.—THE MILITARY COMMISSION. VIENNA, SIINDAY.—The Technical Military Commission which is to proceed to the late, seat of war to delimit a neu- tral zone will set.out immediately, as it is apprehended that the constant skirmishes between the Servian and Bulged:ex outposts might lead to a renawal of hostilities. Five mem- bers of the Commission are the officers acting as attoriteg to the English, French, Garman, Russian, and Italian Embas- sies at Vienna. The Austrian and Turkish Governments will appoint special military delegates. The first queation they will have to deal with will in all probability be the evacuation of the district of Widdin. The next point that will come under their consideration will be whether or not the Bulgarians shall he called upon to withdraw from Ser- vian territory pending negotiations fer an armistice. As to the,negotiations for peace between Servia and Bulgaria, they can hardly be carried on independently of the Eastern, Ronmelian question itself. The Tagbiatt has received the following from St. Petersburg :—ln consequence of the per- sonal influence of the Empress Fedorevna, Prince Alexan- der has been restored to favour. It required four months to bring round the Cxer to a conciliatory mood. Bulgarian union new meets with no furthor opposition at the Ruseian Court. The Tag Mat also publishes a telegram from Bet- grade repotting a considerable engagement between the Servians and Bulgarians near Veliki lever, which, after long and bloody fighting, resulted in the defeat of the, Bulgarians. SEXLIN, MONDAY. It is stated to-night that a conspi- racy, originating in Montenegro, has been discovered against the life of King Milan. According to the statements made. the Secretary of the Montenegrin Supreme Court, named Nikola Vukotic, arrived at Paneeova aboutlen days age on his way to Roumania. During his stay ~as is reported to have communicated to an intimate acquiintance residing there particulars of a secret plan, concocted, as alleged be- tween Russia and Montenegro for the formation of a great Servian State, to consist of Servia, Bosnia, Herzegovina, and Montenegro, under Prince :Nikita. Ile also declared that the plan would be carried oat by next May at the latest. At the same time M. Vukotic stated that one as- sassin bad already been hired for a sum of 40,000 rouliles to kill King Milan. The Servian Government had also heard of the conspiracy from other sources, and informed the King at NifiCh. BELGRADE, MONDAY.—Tbirty appointments of officers were eigced yestei day by Colonel Franassovics, the Servian War Minieter. Several or the new officers are Austrians. A number of persons holding situations here were unex- pectedly called ont for military service yesterday. Though it is geeerally believed that there will he no more fighting between Servia and Bulgaria, werlike preparations continue without interruption. Troops arrive daily from the iaterior, and are despatched to ths front. CONSTANTINOPLE, SATDRDAY.—The Porte to-day com- municated to the Ambassadors of the Powers its objections to the proposal for an Europlian Congress with the object of remodelling the Treaty of Berlin. Nrscrr, SATURDAY.—A favourable reply has been returned by the Powers to the request of tha Servian Government ' for an International Armistice and Demarcation Committee. Lieuteeant-Coloael Pinter, the Austrian Military At- tache, has gone to Belgrade. The troops continue in their positions, exposed night and day to the piercing cold arid snow. Some, MONDAY. The Prince's reply has just been re- ceived. His Highness insists upon the necessity of driving the Servians out of the Widdin district it they persist in evading a settlement and putting forward various pretencee for the rake of gaining time. The Prince farther states th it if the Powers are sincerely desirous of avoiding a re- sumption of hostilities they will insist upon Servia coming to a speedy understanding and evacuating Bulgarian terri- tory. So lone, however, as Servians remain on Bulgarian soil the Prince ref cotes to negotiate, but promises to at once do so with the Military Commission on any reason- able basis once the Servians have retired within their own frontiers.

div.head: PEACE ARRANGEMENTS.
div.p: THE PEACE ARRANGEMENTS.

- WEnNrsDAY.—A large number of villages have to-day followed the example of Yalijevo by sending deputations to King Milan, begging him to continue the war against the Bulgarians on account of what are des- cribed as the high-handed demands of Prince Alexander, and to call upon the country for another effort in order to reach Sofia. _ _

CONSTANTINOPLE, WEDNESDAY. - The Porte yesterday desparched a Circular Note to the Powers in reference to the mission of Lebil Effendi and Gadban Effendi, ex- plaining that the sitnation in Eastern Rournelia was pre- carious.

Puturmorous, WEIDNESDAY.—Madjid Pasha, the Turk- ish special envoy to Prince Alexander, passed through here early this morning on his way to Sofia. VIENNA, WEDNESDAY.—lntelligence received here states that a Bulgarian note was handed yesterday to the repre- sentatives of the Powers accepting the proposal for a mili- tary Commission of demarcation, but at the same time mak- ing certain reservations. The Bulgarian Government also specially exoresses a wish that the Commissioa should tette the Bulgarian victories fairly into account. THE NILE EXPEDITION.—THE FIGHTING AT MOGRAK EH. •

The following has been received at the War 0131ce : CAIRO, DECEMBER 12TH, 8-30 EX.—Three thousand men attacked the Mograken Fort at 6-15 a.m., and got within hundred yards of the fort. At the same time two guns opened on Lotus and field work opposite Kosheh. Stainer not struck. At the same time heavy musketry fire Opened on Kosheh. Attack in Mograkeh repulsed. Besant reports excellent behaviour of garrison, consisting of two companies 3rd Egyptian army. Casualties, two men killed aud one severely wounded. Enemy withdrew to hale in front alter having occupied Firket villages. This message, sent by heliograph from Kosbeh, is somewhat mutilated, the wire being cut. The following are the casualties which have been telegraphed in connected with the attack on Mo- grakeh, Arc.—The killed two, of Egyptian army; severely wounded, No. 2,223 Private Duncan Mattbeson, and No. 132 Private C. Grey, Carneron Highlanders; slightly wounded, one Egyptian ; died of wounds, No. 1,242 Private T. Far- rington, Cameron Highlanders. Cairo, 81:114DAY Ni.—Yesterday morning the Lotus, while steaming up the Nile, was shelled by the ert,my ardunti the Kosheh forts. Sh 3 was tired upon, and heavily, struck several times. The troops .on board were commanded by Captain Hunter Page, and there was a Canadian voya- geur as pilot. At the same time 3,000 of the enemy, advancing from Firket, 41X miles to 'he north, attacked Mograkeh, near Koalieb, garrisoned by 250 Egyptians, Major Besant commanding. The enemy was repulsed with heavy lose, and withdrew to the neighbouring hills. It is hoped that the entire force of the enemy will soon risk a general engagement. The occupation of Dongola is contemplated. To retire during the present state of affairs would affoet most injuriously British interests. Heavy firing con- tinues. ALEXANDRIA, MONDAY.--The 2nd Battalion Dublin Fusiliers pr..cf-eded to Cairo to-day. The Ist battalion of the same regiment arrived yesterday. It will be relieved by the Dorsetshire Regiment on December 23rd, and will then return home. .

The Press Association states theta wrong draft of Royal Engineers was ordered to leave Chatham on Welneaday for Egypt, to join the corps of Royal Engineers in tie Soudan. The inost advanced sections of the British and Egyptian forcer on the Nile, at altasheh and Kosheb, will be gradually reinforced from Cairo. General Srephenson will take the command within the next few days at Assouan, sad an ad- vance upon Dongola is anticipated, for it has been found that the positions at Kosbeh; where it was intended to draw the frontier of Egypt power, is geographically unsatiefac- tory. The importance of the new Mabdi's advance northwards has been magnified by French newspapers. and the force on the Nile is sufficient to succeesfully meet the enemy. Akhbar learns that the Caliph Abdullah hes ordered every native of the Soudan woo has reached the age of sixteen to join the army, and th the order is everywhere obeyed. It is exoec;e4 that thirty thousand nun will be available for the resumption of operations. The Caliph has also ordered the Sultan of Datfur to send him three thou- sand men. CAIICO,IVEDNESDAY.—CoIoneI Ardagh Will start for the , Upper Nile on Friday next. The rebels continue firing ; upon the Cameron Highlanders at Kosbey from behind sandhilla on the other side of the Nile. They mounted a battery of one gun, which was, however, speedily silenced. Major Chalmers and Lieutenant Cameron have been wounded.

div.head: *HEAVY LOSS OF THE _ENEMY.
div.p: *HEAVY LOSS OF THE _ENEMY.

WADY HAIFA, DIIIILSDAY.—In the demosetration from Kositeh, yesterday evening, the enemy were driven from their advanced positions with great loss. Many of the Arabs were bayoneted. The enemy showed in great force, many of them being armed with rides. Their artillery was in position on the vo‘st bank, but it was silenced by the fire from the fort. Our casualties were—Colonel Hunter, Lieutenant Cameron, and Major Chalmers severely wounded, and two privates slightly wounded. All are do- ing well. Desultory 6.4l:Heir continues throughout the day, and ceases at night. The firing does little harm, as the elevation is very bad. The enemy yesterday strengthened their positions on the east and west bank. General Grem fell, with Captain Butler, inspected Kosheh yesterday. The garrison were in very good splits. Captain Bstler remains at Tirket, and General Greufell returns to. Wady Han to- day. Sir E. Stephenson arrived at Wady Haifa or. Satur- day.
MORE REINFORCENIENTS. CAM% Tunßsn.t.y.—The lg. Battalion a the Roril Fssiliers from Gibraltar, now on its way to Alexandria, will on reaching Egypt immediately proceed to the &madam

MALTA. THURSDAY.—IIer Majesty's troopsbip Himalaya ime arrived here from Alexandria to embark tbe La t Port- shire Regiment, whlch has been c4dered to Egypt. She wilt sail for Alexandria to-morrow. TURKEY AND EGYPT.

CONSTANTINOPLF, tiATURDAY.—A. firomise has been given to Sir William White that liiiikhtar Pasha shall leave for Egypt without delay. Sir William Whits has since Sit H. Woolf's departure been constantly pret- siug for this result, but it WAS only obtained by a threat that if be were not at ence sent Sir H. Woolf would leave Egypt. BURMAH. MANDAL&Y, 1110tiDAY.—The Buddist Archbishop yester- day informed Colonel Slsden that he would assist in every way in pacifying the country. He had notified all district priesta that tbe Epglish would respect their religion, and

had argently implored them to promote peace. King The• bau'e sacred white elephant died on the 6th Met. the burial tailt place La the eemetery on the following day. Many Burineree dignitaries attended the ceremony in state. The re- opening of the river navigation for brinerug produce tends largely to quiet the country. The Olympia to-day steamed towards Bhamo under sealed orders. Mannas, MONDAY.—King Theban arrived here this after- noon on board the Canning. It is believed that be will remain here permanently. ROME, SATIYHDAY.—The Italian Government disavows all I knowledge of the correspondence found at Mandalay relating to a treaty between Italy and Burmah. MASSACRE OF EUROPEANS. MADRAS, WEDNESDAY.—It is authoritatively stated, that King Thebawiwill be sent to Retnipett„ near Arcot. . [FROM TRIG RANGOON, SDAY.—lntelligence has been received from Tummoo, through the Government agent at Muni- poor, that eleven Europeans employed by the Bombay and Burmah Company in the Chindwin forest were mastacred at Kendat, on the Chindwin River, by Burmese soldiers sent from Mandalay in a King's steamer. Their names are Mor- gan. Hill, Roberts, Allen, Moreau, Bretto, Roes, Bates, de Gois, and Ruckstahl (2). Although the intelligence has not been officially confirmed, it is believed both by the Bombay and Burinah Company and by the Government. There seems no reason to doubt the fact, as the report is partially confirmed from ether. sources. SKIRMISHES WITH THE DACOTTS. MANDALAY, TIIORtDAY.—AiLijor Walker, while recon- noitring with an advanced party of Major Collin's column in an easterly direction through setae villager!, was sud- denly attacked by a party of Shea daooita. Major Walker was wounded and a native soldier killed. The Major, ob- serving the number of decoits, fell back on his supports and ordered his men to open fire. &vein of the daooits were killed. • Two squadrons of Madras cavalry have arrived here, and one troop will leave to-day in order to make arrangements with the Weems for keeping the telegraph wires intact. Col. Sladen believes that dacoiting will continue until a settled government has been established. GREECE AND TURKEY. CONSTANTINOPLE, WEDNESDAY.—AIthOtigh M. Condos- rioti, to Greek Minieter, has contradicted the reports , attributing warlike intentions to Greece, the Porte evinces great irritation and suspicion against that country. Con- siderable activity prevails at the Turkish Admiralty, where preparations are being made for the defence of Salonica. FRANCE.--ELECTIONS ANNULLED. PARIS, MONDAY.—The results received up to the present of the six elections in the department of the Seine yester- day show that in 510 sections, out of a total of 830, the Republican and the Radical candidates head the poll with from 86,000 to 71 000 votes. The Chamber of Deputies to- day, by 261 votes to 233, declared the elections in the Be. part ment of Lozere to be invalid, owing to the interference of the clergy. MR. VANDERBILT'S WILL. NEW YORK, SATURDAY.—Mr. Vanderbilt's will Was read yesterday after the funeral. The following are the tes- tamentary distortions :—The house and its contents are left to the widow, tegether with on annuity ol 200,000 dole. and a lump sum of 500,001 dole. Each of the deceesed's eight children receives 10,000,000 dole., and his son Cornelius an additional 2,000 000 dole. The charitable I bequests amount to another million, and the residue of his estate is divided between his two eons Cunelius and Wm. K. Vanderbilt. The testator directs that the railway stocks he bequeaths to hie children shall be held in bulk aod ad- r ministered for the beet interests of all. None of such stock I is to be disposed of without the consent of all concerned. 4 The fortune left by the deceased is generally estimated at I 200,0071,000 .

GREAT FIRE 1N PLDIOUTII. LOSS OF 13 LIVES. A terrible calamity visited Plymouth early on Sunday morning, by which thi, teen persons, many of them children, loot their lives. A fire breke out in Dire. 3, Looe-street, in the very heart of Old Plymouth. Looe-street is a very narrow thoroughfare leading from Whimple-street to Veux- hall-street, and the premises in question are situered a few yards down the bill at tne top ot which stands the Navel Bank and the Old Guiidtall, the latter now used as a Free Library. Almost all the houses are old and crowded with tenants, families of seven or eight persous occupying one , or two rooms. The premises burnt down were separated from the adjoining property by stout walls, and there was no wind. The destruction of property was therefore small, but the loss of life makes the calamity one of the heaviest ever experienced in the town. The house was once a pub- lishing office of a newspaper, but had been converted into a double house with a centrrl passage, the ground floor be- ing occupied by ahopkeepera and two upper floors let out in tenements. Altogether the inmates of the ill-fated house numbered 31. Mr. Sprague, butcher, owner, occupied the shop on the left-hand side of the passage and a room behind, with a bedroom on the first floor. Ms family consisted of his wife and two children. The lower shop was rented by a widow named Bahhage who also occupied two bedrooms, and with her were lodg- ing her brother. Edmund Downing, and Mrs. Kirby, sieter to Downing. The back apartments, on the first floor were oecuided by Mr. and Mrs. Davey and four children. On the upper floor three families were located. The front rooms were occupied by a family named Foss. The other mem- bers of this family were Mrs. Foss, four girls named Lizzie, Minnie, Lily, Flurry, and three boys—William, Alfred, and John. A Mrs. Newcombe and her daughter Amy. a young child, occupied another room on the same fiat, and the two rooms behind were tenanted by a widow named Jane Bick- ford, her five children, and a lodger named Daniel. Mrs. Bickferd's children were Edward, aged 20; William, 18;' Frank, 14 ; Frederick, 11 ; and Alfred, 9. Out of the 31 I persons enumerated twelve were dead alter the fire had been got under. Fen's wife and the whole if her seven children I wore suffocated in their beds, the other victims being Fred.l Bickford, Mrs. Sprague, Mrs. Kirby, and Downing, her brother. Foss jumped from the top storey while the fire was raging, and sustained such fearful injuries that it is scarcely possible he can recover. Mr. Sprague saved his' two children, and was under the impression, until too late, that his wife had made her escape. The Davey family were rescued by ladders from the windows at the rear, and the Bickford family were saved by similar means, except one little fellow named Frederick, who gut separated from the rest of the family and was subsequently found in a front room. The fire broke out shortly after one o'clock, when a seaman named Maloney observed the glimmer of a light between the shut- ters of Mrs. Bibbages shop. Maloney raised an alarm, and commenced to tear down the shutters. A Iran living oppo- site was aroused by hie wife, and ruebed to the police station. The hose reel was got out, and with all the men available proceeded to the scene, but by the time It arrived the flames had complete hold of the building. The remains of five of the children, dreadfully charred, were found In one I bed. Mrs. Sprague's bedyiwas found half under the bed-! Subsequently came the discovery of Downing and his sister, Mrs. Kirby, in the bedroom if the former, and the boy Bickford. Those who escaped were I almost without exception clad only in their night garb mente, and were dependent upon neighbours for shelter and clothing. An inquest was held on Monday evening. The jury re- turned a verdict of " Accidental death,' &Vine. a rider recognieing the self-sacrifice of Mrs. Kirby (who lost her life while endeavouring to arouse other inmates of the building), and stating that, in their opinion, everything was done to save life that could poesi- Ny be done.

TUEBDAY.—A. terrible accident occurred to- day on the Georgia and Pacific Railway, a collision occur- I ring between two trains about fifteen miles from Atalanta. I A sleeping car was demolished, twelve of the passengers I being killed outright and thirteen injured, three so seri- ously that their lives are despaired of. PantEgrower V. STANLEY (LivEnnom.)—The meeting of these crack " teams at Eartestown on Saturday after- noon occasioned great excitement in football circles. The match was played on the Mesnes, the ground of the Liver- pool and District Cupholders, and notwithstanding the un- settled character of the weather there was a large attend- ahce ot spectators, who were rewarded by witnessing a bril- liantlytconteated and highly exciting game. The visitors' appeared without Dick, while the only absentee from the home team was Rich, whose place was filled by Ho!croft. The groend was in a very slippery condition, which eon ee- q uen tl y made the kicking somewhat uncertain. Having won the toss the Earlestown captain (Dagnall) eelected to play with the ground in his favour. Highett set the ball in motion for Stanley, and it was taken to the Earlestown quar- ters, but the brothers Green cleared, and play was transferred to mid-field, when Ellison scored the premier point about a quarter of an hour from the start amid loud cheers. Shortly after the recommencement the home team made a rush for the visitors' citadel, and from the scrimmage Dagnall scored the second goal amid renewed cheers. The brothers Wit. son now relieved the pressure, and shot the ball just outside the Earlestown goal. Sims was prominent with a run, and , then Ellison beat the Stanley custodian a third time. After I this the visitors played up with considerable dash, and had rather hard Hoes in not scoring. Dagnall, however, came to the front, and registered a fourth goal for Earleston. which I brought half-time. On the resumption of hostilities the I game was very fast aad exciting. The Stanley left made a dashing :mu down the field, placing a shot in the mouth of the gnat, frost which they scored their first and only goad. Earlestown then visited the Stanley quarters, and from a scrimmage they notched their fifth goal. Directly after this the whistle announced time, when Earlestown had secured a splendid victory by fire goals to one.. Teams:— I Stanley : G. Wright, troal ; It. Stephenson sort G. Dovey. backs; 11. The visitors came with an unbeaten certificate, and Warrington had arranged to play their cap team. The home arrangement", Nowever. failed, as two Players were unable to get up in time. Roberti at half hack was much wanted, and his judicious play would, no doubt, have made a different result possible. J. The score at half time eteod War- rington one god, four corners, to nil. Immediattly after re'terting Hamilton stopped a wonderful shot from White, and Gledhill scored from a mis-kick by the goalkeeper. The epeetatare applauded tho right wings, White and Wilson, for a tine bit of passing, but Hind interposed, and with a I long kick put his forwards in poeseesion. Parker shot, but I Gamble saved, and a claim for " hands " was given to the home team in front of goal. Wigan played up well, but were forced to concede two more corners and the game ended in a victory for the home team. - - _ King Frost was abroad last week, which caused the prin- cipal clubs in the various shires to abandon their matches. True a slight thaw set in on Friday, but his Majesty had got too firm a hold to be easily removed. The only match of any note was that played at Liverpool between the Old Boys of that city and Wiaan, and although the Old Boys had whlpped together a pretty strong team, the Wiganers proved too strong for them by oce goal and two ininars to one minor. _ . .

tVirines received a visit from the Birch Club, who came short banded, bur suisstitutes having to be found for them. At call of time Widnes were the victors by one goal, one try, and two minors to nil. Carley is improving wonderfully , in his passing. The principal topic of conversation in football circles has been the selection of the teams for the North v. South match, which will be played to-day on the Bradford ground. It caused some astonishment in the MAnchester district when it, was known that Leggin, of Broughton, had not been thought good enough for the North team, and Cheshire are waxing wroth, not baying a single representative on the teun when they have such a man as .galls. Both teams are almost as strong as it is possible to make them, and a ! grand exposition of Rugby football is sure to bewitnessed. During the past few years the southern team have managed to defeat the North, but to,lay there is reason to think that the northern team will just about account for the southern, _

TRE INETIIERBY JFAVEL ROBBERY.—The Cumberland police have made an important discovery in connection with the jewel robbery which took place at Netherby on October 28th. When the prieontr Wedge and his two corn' 'anions jumped out of the goods train at Telety Station, after the murder of P.C. Byrnes at Plnmpten, he took re- fuge under an arch of the bridge which crosses the river Lune at the north side of Tebay Station, He was pursued by the railway men and captured while attempting to draw a revolver from his pocket. A few days afterwards, a dia- mond eatdrop, part.of the stolen property, was found near the spot, acd the bnpreesion created Was that the prisoner had attempted to throw the jewel into the river, but it had fallen short. On Saturday mornine, P.C. Scott found, on . the bask of the river near the railway bridge at Tebay, bat • on the opposite side of the ricer to that on which Hedge was ' taken, three diamond stars, one diamond eardrop and a finger ring, which formed port of the stolen property ; and it may now be said that the jewels which have been found constitute the whole of the missing property, ' except a email enamelled gold watch key and a framed pho- tograph.

CONSTABLIC—At the Liverpool City Sessions on Wednesday, Michael Dobbin, a police-constable, was charged with having, in the bridewell at Rosa Hill, Liverpool, on the 4th instant, assaulted Thomas Edward Groves. of Anfield. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 19, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 19, 1885.

"THE Financial Reform Almanack" for 1386 has jnst been issued, and we are glad to see that, notwithstanding the passing of the Reform Bill, there is no sign of any fall- ing off in the interest or value of its pages. The Almanack has hid much to do, more than the ordinary observer may think, in bringing about the great constitutional change which has resulted not only in a large I extension of the franchise, but in a redistri- bution of seats on a thoroughly radical basis. In season and out of season, it has been the means of bringing before the public the most glaring anomalies in representation, its tables of electoral statistics being extensively made use of by speakers of all kinds. The ex- posures of late years of the we ik places in our land laws have not unnaturally alarmed and irritated those who would like to let things alone ; and there has been a syste- matic attempt on the part of certain Tory orators to discredit the authority of the Almanack. Some of the leading Fair Traders have been especially active in this direction, for there is nothing they so much dislike as a solid phalanx of facts. Allow them to theorise at large, and they make what the Yankees call a "fair show ;" bring them to book as to facts in any particular case and it is instantly seen that they have been building castles in the air. Lord STANLEY of Alderley, who is, or was, Presi- dent of the Fair Trade League, made light of a statement found in the Almanack to the effect that " the corn land of the kingdom ght, without strain, by the application Of nitrate, be made to produce an additional Wheat crop." He thought he had caught the editor following the example of his lordship --that is talking about something he did not understand; but it was Lord STANLEY of

Alderley who stood exposed when it tran- spired that the statement was backed up by Sir JAALEs CAIRD, who is generally regarded as the greatest living authority on the land question. Sir CHARLES CRAUFORD seconded his lordship's efforts in trying to weaken the Association ; but the result of their " writing privately and publicly for six months " is that the list of Vice- eresidents "is now far larger than ever before in the history of the Association." Turning to the contents of the new volume, we find that the spaces set at liberty by the re- moval of the tables on the representation of Ithe people are well occupied. The Clergy have thought fit to raise the question of" the Church" as a battle cry, and they cannot complain if they find that the Almanack betters their instruction. Articles on " The State Church" cover about a score of pages of the present issue. To begin with, we have a brief account of the votes of the Bishops in the House of Lords. We have always thought the Bishops were—politically spEaki•tg--1 bad lot, but we were scarcely prepared for such an indictment against them as these pages present. The Bishops opposed a Bill having for its object the abolition of capital pun- ishment for thefts from shops ; they op- posed all bills going in the direction of national education ; they opposed Catnolic lemancipation again and again; th y opposed the Reform Bill of 1831 and 1832 ; they opposed the Jewish Disabilities Repeal Bill— not foreseeing that they would eventually have to bow down to a Jew as Prime Minister; they opposed the abolition of Universi.y tests; they opposed the abolition of Church rates; they opposed the Burials Bill ; and they stand in the way to-day of the passing of the Marriage with a Deceased Wife's Sister Bill—a measure demanded by the nation, dic- tated by common sense, and supported by Scripture. There is no absurdity they have not sanctioned; there is no tyranny they have not upheld. They have done evil, and that continually, in the House of Lords; and the first step in the way of reform of that House should be the removal from it of the bench of Bishops. The articles in the Almanack on "Church and State " deal, amongst other things, with the nature .of Ecclesiastical resources, first fruits and tithes, the landed possessions of the Church, the state of things before Par- liamentary reform, coal duties to build churches, patronage, and sale of livings ; and for those who want a nut to crack there is '"A Method of Disendowment for England and Wales." There is a long list of rich I livings where, in many cases, the people are poor and the population sparse. The livingi of Hempstead. in the diocese of Gloucester and Bristol, is put down in CROCKFORD'S list as worth £l,OOO per year ; and in this case. happily for the parson, the pounds are more , plentiful than the people, for the population is just 412. At St. Margaret's (London) there is a population of 361, while the income is £960. But there is a worse case than this, or shall we say a better ? it is all a question of the point of view. The living of St. Andrew Undershaft and St. Mary Axe (Lon- don) is given as being worth £2,373 per year. The population numbers 327. counting man, woman, and child The Clergy doubtless know what they are about in countenancing such abuses. Who wouldn't be a curer of souls with a chance of being paid for the work, year by year, at the rate of over £7 per head, big and little? There is, of course, a dark side of the picture. and that is revealed in such cases as that of St. Clement's (Sal- ford), with a population of 13,307, and a living of Lip per year; and St. George's (Camberwell), with a similar income, to a population of 2o,+r S. There are people who will say that both sides of the picture are dark, and that the Financial Reform Associ- ation is doing good work in letting the light in. No one can hear of these and other anomalies of Church and State without feel- ing that there is a need for reform. What laymen in the Church require to learn, how- ever, is that the Clergy as they are at pre- sent situated are too strong for them—that they cannot have Reform without Disestab- lishment.

THERE was "a bit of a row" about politics at Earlestown just before the . election; and it ended, as rows often do, in the appearance of the principals before the magistrates. It would seem from the evidence given in the Newton Police Court on Saturday, that WILLIAM JENNINGS and JAMES FAGAN are both employed at the London and North- Western Railway Company's waggon works at Earlestown. They were walking together at noon on Nov. z7th along with another man, when JENIIINGS took to denouncing PARNELL and all his works, including FAGAN as a Parnellite in the bargain. JENNINGS was knocked down for his too free expression of opinion; hence the charge of assault which was preferred against FAGAN. The latter made an ingenious defence; and, as it proved successful, it will be invaluable to people who have an inclination to use their fists, but, at the same time, don't like to pay for the privilege. FAGAN disputed in the first place that he knocked JENNINGS down ; but he admitted that, after hearing certain language, "his hand went up and struck the complainant, but he knew not how Lit went and he could not help it." There could anything be more perfect in the way of a defence? FAGAN in fault? Not a bit of it. He was a passive spectator of the whole proceedings. It was his hand that went up and struck . JENNINGS down; he could not help it ; and who will say that any human being is responsible for doing that which he cannot help? Not the Newton Bench of Magistrates, who were powerfully impressed with this mode of reasoning, for they finally dismissed the case. Henceforth it will be necessary to distinguish, at election time, between a man and his hand. And what an opportunity it will give for hard-hitting all round ; for, of course, what is sauce for the goose will be sauce for the gander. If the Parnellite bruiser can escape scot free by laying the blame on the hand that would strike, a like defence will surely hold good for the Anti-Parnellite, and'everybody will be happy and black-eyed. This is, to be sure, a very nice arrangement, but we can not help wondering how it was that the Newton magistrAtes did not fine" that hand," or take it into custody, seeing that there was not a shadow of doubt as to its guilt. Can it be that they were afraid that "that hand" would again go up and strike, and that nobody would be responsible for it ? If a band that writes on a wall, at a King's feast, is terrible, how much more terrible must be the hand that goes up and knocks a man down?

ME approach of Christmas brings with it, amongst other things, a revival of lotteries, or "Christmas draws" as they are popularly termed. They are illegal, of course, and the police, in some parts of the country, are put- ting them down. At Crewe, a 'timber of

tradesmen have been fined for exhibiting tickets in their windows for these Christmas lotteries; and at Lambeth, London, a trades- man has been brought to account in a similar way. The proceedings were taken under the Act previously quoted in these columns in discus§ing this subject, namely, that which deals with the offenders as " rogues and vagabonds." It may be that the law requires amending—most likely it does ; but what most needs amending is the mode of enforc- ing it We protest. as we have protested before, against the Act remaining a dead letter so far as lotteries at bazaars are con- cerned, while it is enforced against publi- cans and other tradesmen who may have " Christmas draws." It is grossly inconsis- tent in magistrates to take part in bazaar lot- teiies one month, and before the year is out have a voice in fining men who may sin as they have sinned, but in a less degree. If it is a breach of the law to draw for a goose at Christmas, it is equally a breach of the law to draw for a screen or a picture, at a bazaar, during any other part of the year. It is not sufficient to suggest that the man who takes a ticket for a draw at a public house must be something of a goose himself; for the retort is obvious that many a goose has been plucked at a Fancy Fair. If lotteries are to be nut down, let them be put down all round; let us not have one law for the rich and another for the poor.

THE MAYOR OF WARRINGTON (Alderman ! JOSEPH HARRISON) is showing himself especi- shy and thoughtful at Christmastide. He has followed the custom, as Chief Magi- strate, in giving a dinner during his years of office to the members and officials of the Corporation ; but this year, in view of the !distress which exists in some parts of the • town, he intends to go a little further. He l has decided to give a dinner of good " Hot Pot" on Christmas Day to no less than 1500 persons (with their children) who may !be out of work or in distress. The dinner, as will be seen from our advertising col- umns, will be given in the Drill Hall, Bath- street; and provision will be made for supplying those who, for various reasons, may not be in a position to have their repast at the hall. Care will, of course, be taken to see that the tickets get into proper hands, and it is to be hoped that the deserv- ing poor will render what assistance they can in this respect, so that there may be no abuse of his Woßstur's bounty. The MAYOR is not a rich man, and his generous conduct is therefore the more -deserving of praise. He has set an example in the way of giving good cheer to such as cannot provide for themselves which may well be followed. Those who cannot giv,- a dinner may he able to give a trifle here and there. They can hardly go wrong so long as they do not offer intoxicants. They will not enjoy their own Christmas any the less if they make somebody else happy besides themselves.
THE FXAMINER. SATURDAY, DECEMBER 19, 1885.

div.head: OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATION.
div.p: OUR ALMANAC ILLUSTRATION.

KNOWSLEY HALL AND TIIE DERBY FAMILY. To-day we present each purchaser of "The Examiner" with a large Sheet Almanac, which, as will be seen, contains a large stock of local and general information, and is adorned with a view of Knowsley Hall, the seat of the Right Hon. the Earl of Derby.

The three Portraits placed beside the view of Knowsley Hall are (as the reader will doubtless recognise) those of (1) Edward Geoffrey Smith- Stanley, K.G., &c., 14th Earl, born 29 March, 1799; married 31 May, 1825; M.P. for Preston (1826-30), Windsor, and North Lancashire ; ;n 1844, summoned to the House of Lords in his father's barony; suc- ceeded to the Earldom on his father's death, 30 June, 1851; Prime Minister of England in 1852, 1858, and 1866 ; died 23 October, 1869, aged 70. (2) Edward Henry Stanley, 15th and preaent Earl of Derby; born 21 July, 1826, many years M.l'. for Kings Lynn; succeeded to the Earldom 23 October, 1869; married 5 July, 1870;• no issue; Foreign Secretary in the Beaconsfield Government, and Colonial Secretary in the Gladstone Government. (3) Frederick Arthur Stanley, brother and pre- sumptive heir of the preseht Earl; born 15 January, 1811 ; married 31 May, 1864, and has issue five soils; M.P. for Preston (1865-68), and for North Lanca- shire (1868-85); Secretary for War in the Beacons- ' field Government, and Colonial Secretary in the present Government. 11 We are indebted to the columns of " The Preston Guardian " for the following interesting historical : account of Knowsley Hall, and the Derby family. It lis close upon five centuries since the manor and. ' manor-house of Knowsley passed into the posses- sion of the Stanleys, by the marriage of Sir John Stanley, Rut., with Isabella, elder of the three daughters of Sir Thomas Lathom, Ent., lord of Lathom, Knowsley, &c. If we could fix the exact year of this acquisition it would be interesting. The matter is left very vague in the " History of Lancashire " and.other authorities ; but the late ' Mr. William Langton investigated carefully the de- , scendants of the last of the De Lathoms, and from the facts he has deduced from inquisitions, patent rolls, &c., we are able to assert that it was between the years 138.7 and 1390 that .Isabel, wife of Sir John de Stanley, became next heir to the paternal estates. Her father, Sir Thomas de Lathom, died, after an illness of about three months, at "Ktioices- legh," early in 1382, and is recorded to have been hastily hnd unceremoniously buries at Burscough Priory, his second wife Joanna being a person of very indifferent character. Sir Thomas's son and heir, Thomas de Lathona,Esq., held possession of the estates only about a year and a half, and died the 3rd November, 1383. That is just over 500. years ago; and it has been assumed that he died without issue, in which case his sister Isabel would have been his heir. But Mr. Langton has printed docu- ments which prove that he left an infant daughter, Ellena, born about the end of January, 1384 (nearly three months after her father's death). This child was the ward of Henry, Duke of Lancaster, and seems to lave been alive in 1387, but was dead be- fore 1390. It is not unlikely that Sir John Stanley had entered into the estates at Lathom before the infant heiress of Thomas de Lathom deceased; but at any rate this scion of the house of Stanley was lord of Lathom and Knowsley somo time before 1390. In 1408, Henry IV. granted to Sir John de Stanley to have a "saltus"- within the "park at Knoweslegh ;" so that the Knowsley demesne had been emparked prior to that date. Sir John Stanley was made a Knight of the Garter on the accession of Henry V. (1413), and died in 1414. His wife, the Knowsley heiress, survived him a short time; made a settlement of her estate 12th March, 1414, and died the 26th October, 1414. 'Her son and heir, John de Stanley, was aged 28 years at the time of his mother's decease. . He was the first of the Stanleys who held Knowsley in his own right by inheritance from his mother. For nearly a century after the Stanleys possessed these valuable domains on the great western plain 'of Lancashire, Lathom House remained their accustomed seat, as it had been that of their predecessors in ownership, the De Lathoms. Knowsley was kept as a' hunting lodge and chase and the lodge would probably consist of a single square tower standing in the midst of the park. The John Stanley who succeeded his mother in 1414, at the age of 28, was afterwards knighted, and he was father of Sir Thomas Stanley, created Baron Stan- ley, and grandsire of Thomas, second Lord Stanley, who, in 1485, so powerfully helped Henry Tudor, Earl of Richmond, to win the battle of Bosworth and to secure the English Crown. This Thomas. Lord Stanley, had married, for his second wife, Margaret, Countess of Richmond, mother of Henry the Seventh; so he was in the relation of s'epfather to that monarch, who, shortly after his accession, had created Lord Stanley an Earl, with the title of Earl of Derby (27th October, 1485), and given him several forfeited eitates of adherents of Richard 111. Although Heriry the Seventh had caused Sir William Stanley of Holt, the brother of this first Earl of Derby, to be beheaded in 1494, on the suspicion (apparently groundless) of complicity in the insurrection of Perkin Warbeck, this family ' tragedy did not stand in the way of an invitation

_ being given to 1 the King, and accepted, to visit the Earl of Derby at his Lancashire seats, in June, 1496. In preparation for this great event the Earl built at Knowsley an extension to the hunting lodge, con- sisting, it is said, of a detached stone building, with two round towers, in which the King was enter- tained, and perhaps lodged, during some portion of his visit to the Earl. Lathom was, however, still the Earl's principal mansion; and it was at Lathom, not at Knowsley, that the incident mentioned in Kennett's MSS. occurred. When the King had gone over the Muse at Lathom, the Earl conducted him to the roof over the largest of the towers to view the landscape. The Earl's jester was along with the King and Earl, and observing the King standing near the edge a the roof, muttered to his master • Tom, remember Will"—hinting that the Han l had a good chance then given him of avenging his brother William's death, by casting the King down from the tower. Lord Derby owed too much to Henry the Seventh to dream of acting upon the jester's hint, but the legend runs that the King heard-the words of the jester, or guessed their pur- port, and lost no more time in descending from the tower, and, indeed, quitted Lathom as soon 'as he conveniently could. From the date of the exten- sions of . the manor-house of Knowsley, about 1494-95, the Harts of Derby have always, we believe, made Knowsley one of their ordinary residences, and after the demolition of Lathom House during the Civil War, and for more than two centuries now, Knowsley has been the-one great Lancashire house of the family; although the Earls of Derby long kept a town house in Church-street, Pre-stot. "In 1552," writes Mr. Draper, in his interesting Memoirs of the House of Stanley, " the Knowsley estate was greatly increased iby Edward, the third Earl of Derby, who received n exchange for his house in London, called Derby Place, considerable lands ad- joining the old domain of Knowsley." The family had, in the time of the third and •fourth Earls, another.seat in this county called Altom Castle, or the New Park, situate on the Lathont estate, about half a mile from Lathom HOllBB. In December,ls66, Earl Henry has recorded inlis Household Book : --- "On Satoreday the housßolde removed from Knowsley to the new Parke." Knowsley township and manor are situated in the parish of Huyton, but the nearest town is Pres- cot, beyond the south-eastern boundary of the es- tate. The Park of Knowsley is the largest in the county, andas circuit is about thirteen miles. ilt is entered by eleven separate gateways, flanked by as many elegant lodges. The principal lodge is at the entrance from the direction of Liverpool, and consists of a bold central archway, supported by a round tower on the right and a square tower on the left. The grounds within the park are pleasantly undulated, and the more elevated spots command beautiful prospects to the westward. There is no lack of pine trees in the park, but the gales from the seawlird cause the timber to grow less symmet- rically in West Lancashire than in some inland counties. The glades and avenues of Knowsley are, notwithstanding, charming and noble. The present Earl is exceedingly liberal in permitting large par- ties of townspeople to have their holiday excursions to Knowsley, whereby thousands of industrious workers are enabled to enjoy its beauties. The "Large Lakes' in the park is a sheet of water cover- ing ninety acres of ground, and there are two other artificial lakes in the grounds, one of which Surrounds the south and east fronts of the hall. The gardens and terraces are beautifully laid out, and to the floral splendours (in the summer season) are added the attractions of art, in the shape of striking groups of sculpture.' The Deer Park contains numerous herds of red and fallow deer. -

The Hall of Knowsley, which forms the subject of the engraving in our Almanac, is, as the picture shows, an edifice of imposing proportions, but of mixed architectural styles. Here we see the Gothic form of English domestie architecture of the Tudor period standing in juxtaposition with Italian archi- tecture as understood by English architects in the early years of last century. It would, no doubt,. have been much more effective and harmonious hid the later extensions of the mansion bee4designed in keeping with the older erections. But classic was the rage in this country when James, tenth Earl of Derby, built the newk wing to Knowsley Hall which is to the right of our picture, behind the handsome facade with its double-Storied colonnade. This Earl held the estates, in succession to his brother, from November, 1702, till his deatth in February, 1735-6, and it was during the few last years of his posses- sion that the major parts of the existing fabrics were built or altered. These works were completed in 1732, which is the date appended to an inscribed stone tablet, seen beneath the arms of the Stanleys, in the centre of the parapet above the upper colon- nade, bearing these words :—" James, Earl of Derby, Lord of Man and the Isles, Grandson of James, Earl of Derby, and of Charlotte, daughter of Claude Duke de hi. Tremouille, whose Husband, James, was be- headed at liolton. 15th • October, 1652, for strenu- ously adhering to Charles the Second, who refused a Bill passed unanimously by both Houses of Parliament for restoring to the Family the Estate lost by his loyalty to him. 1732." A full des- cription of the Hall we cannot pretend to give in this short sketch, We abridge from Mr. Draper's. acount the following :—The mansion consists -of two sides of a square. The west front is built of red brick, with stone dressings to the, long range of windows, and, though modernised in exter- nal aspect, it includes some of the oldest portions of the Hall. In the centre of this extensive block is the main entrance, reached by a double flight of steps leading to the principal floor. In this build- ing are contained the spacious drawing-rooms and the noble picture gallery. The east front is also built of red brick, with stone dressings, and is pierced bidong ranges of 'windows. Near the centre a projecting wing forms the domestic chapel, en- tered from the interior of the house. This eastern frontage, which is longer than the western. termi- nates at one extremity in the south colonade front, and at the other with the rooms north of the library, in which the grandfather of the present Earl had his Museum, now the property of the Corporation of Liverpool. On this east front are displayed the Derby and Hesketh arms; the date 1704' and the inscription "Edward and Elizabeth, Earl and Countess of Derby." The south front is that pre- sented in our Almanac illustration, and is built of red stone. It has three distinct parts; first, the colonnaded front, which masks the gable of the east block; second, the massive square tower, with its embattled parapet and angle turrets, seen in the middle of the picture, the interior of which is the great banqueting hall; and next, to the left, the buildings of Tudor architecture with the arcade in front of the lower storey, and with the two em- battled towers rising `above the roof-line. These last-named structures, as originally built by Thomas Stanley, first Earl, were detached from. the older house, and contained a dining-room' a drawing- room, staircase, and bed chambers above for the King, his chamberlain, page, &c.; they were called the King's Apartments. The south end was re- fronted in stone by Edward, twelfth Earl, in 1821, when he was preparing to receive the Prince Regent. It is the most impressive exterior view of the man- sion. The colonnaded portion projects considerably beyond the line of the square tower and the other buildings on the left, and is certainly the most pala- tial feature of the hall, whatever may be said of its architectural incongruity. Over anentrance, in the building to the left of this south front, has been in- serted a fragment of the original structure, which is a stone on which are sculptured the badges of the Stanley Family—the Eagle's Claw erased, and the Three Legs conjoined, armed, and spurred—the latter the badge of the Kings of Man. At the north end of the hall is a wing from the west front, of two storeys; the lower storey containing the larders, storerooms, &c., and the upper the Bachelors' Apartments. This wing is built of red stone. The series of family portraits is most interesting; and the Library, besides a valuable collection of rare books, ptints, and manuscripts, contains one relic of special interest. It is an old oak chair, with a low curved back and spiral spindles; on a silver plate fixed in the back is inscribed :—" This Chair of the Great Earl of Derby at his maiityrdom was presented by James Hardcastle, of Bolton-le-Moors. Esq., to the Right Hon. Edward-Geoffrey, Earl of Derby." The Stables and Coachhouse at Knowsley were.built about the year 1850 by the grandfather of the present Earl, at a cost of £30,000, and are not only the largest and finest private stables in Lanca- shire, but perhaps in England. They stand a short distance from the mansion, at the north end. Her Majesty Queen Victoria and the Prince Con- sort, on their visit to Lancashire in October, 18,51, alighted from the 'train at% Prescot, and drove through Knowsley Park to Croxteth Hall, the seat of the Earl of Sefton. Her Majesty thought Knows- ley Park " very fine," and wrote in her Journal, "It reminded us of Windsor.'

SHAW AND THE RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.—COD I several recent occasions the Rencorn School Board bevel utilized the Board-room of the Board of Commiseioaers for I their meetings in consequence of the Inability of the Rev. Canon Barclay to ascend the stairs to the rooms of the educa- tional body. The members of the School Board were surprised on Saturday morning to find that the doors If the room were locked, and for some time they consulted in the passage what should be done as the respected Vicar's bath chair mild not possibly be conveyed upstairs. Whilst they were considering Mr. Robert Slaw, chairman of the Board of Commiseioners, appeared en the scene, and mentioned that the Board-room bad been twice used without permis- sion. He thought that so long as they had commodious premises of their own in the saute building they ought not to make such an encroachment. The circumstances were explained, and Mr. Sbew intimated that they might use th 3 room that morning. The door was subsequently unlocked, and the Board transacted their business. THE DASTARDLY OUTRAGE ON RUNCORN BRIDGE. A meeting of the Runcorn' branch of the Irish National League was held in the "Friendship Tavern," Fryer-street, Runcorn, on Tuesday evening. A good number attended, end Mr. John Kelly was in the chair. After the usual rou- tine business, the following resolution was proposed by Mr. Peter Noon, and seconded by Mr. Ryan, "That we, the members of the Runcorn Branch of the Irish National League, do condemn, in the strongest possible language, the recent villainous outrage on Mr. Edward Hill, the presi- dent, and pronounce their opinion that no 'lrishman in Run- corn belonging to the leegue would lay a finger on him with intent to do him any harm." It was carried unanimously. Mr. Hill, on being interviewed, gave it as his candid opin- ion that no member of the league in Runcorn had anything to do with the outrage. and he believes that no Irishman in Runcorn would be guilty of so base a crime, as his conduct with regard to the recent election bad been explained by him at a former meeting or the branch and accepted. Hill's condition still' causes some anxiety among his friends. It is generally accepted that the attack upon him was a private feud, but the police have not as yet made any arrests. BgruesPA CHAPEL, licwoonle : MISSIONARY MEETING The annual sermons in aid of the London Missionary , Society were preached by the Rev. E. II Stripling, a re- turned missionary from Madagascar, on Sunday morning and evening. On Tuesday evening the annual missionary meeting was held in the Schoolroom. Mr. Thomas Hand- ley occupied the chair, and delivered a brief and appropri- ate address. The Rev. E. H. Seripting gave an interesting account of b;s labours in Madagascar, and of the rapid strides that country had made rewards a fell and complete acceptance of the Christian faith, concluding with a power- ful appeal for help. The Rev. W. Lee, from South India, spoke of the results of missionary labour in India. For 91 rears the London Missionary Society had been at work, and there were in India 91,497 Church 'members as a result of the lehours of their missionaries. (Applause.) There were also 325,1,71 pereens who were members of the Christian congregations of the London Missionary Society in India. (Applause.) He contended ,that these results amply repaid them for their labours, and added that in India there were 250,000.000 people, and only 600 missionaries. Truly the harvest was plenteous, but the labourers were few. Be described his labours amongst the people. and dealt with the difficulties of converting them in consequence of the acceptance of the Christian faith involving a less of caste, and often times the loss of the nearest and dearest relatives. Urging those present to be more generous in their aid to the missionaries, he said the mere Christians there were In India and the more loyal that country would be to England. Mr. William Handley, after narrating the important part the missionary meetings formerly played in the religious life of Bethesda Chapel, read the report. The collections for the Widows and Orphans' Fund was LI 13s Sd ; at the public services and that evening, £5 las Sal; Bethesda school (New Year offerings), £6 163 ; school boxes, £2 25,, 6d ; St. Luke's school boxes, £2 4s ; subscription to deficiency fund by Mr. James Handley, J.P., £3 Sc; Mrs Handley, Ll is; Mr. J. Williams, Li; T. B. Handley 's missionary box, £l4s fid ; total contributed to the society, £25 3s lop. On the motion of the Rey. J. D. Thomas. seconded by Mr. F. Beck, a vote of thanks was accorded the deputation, and a like compliment having been paid to the chain:ban, the proceedings concluded.
