Murray, of Preston, and Bro. Shenton, of -Sutton. AN INCORRIGIBLE TRUANT AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty cessions, on Wednesday, Mr. G. H. Denby applied , on behalf of the School Board for George Carr, 11 years of I age, son of James Carr, who liras in Queen-street. to be I committed to an Industrial School.—From the atetement Of Mr. Hanby and the evidence of the School Attendance Officer Joynson, it appeared ,that the boy, who appeared In a very diry condition, was utterly beyond the control of his father. For days together he would never put in an ap- pearance at home, and although it had been desired en several occasions to bring him before the magistrates, he could never be found. It was only by the aid of the police that be was caught on the present occasion. His father had paid £8 in fines.— The bey was committed to the Liv-rpool Certified Industrial School. ' A Womerr's Anverrrune AT WIDNES —About half-past eight on Saturday night Richard Grant, caretaker of the Warrington-road Board schools, beard screams ('I" Murder' proceeding from a fi.ld some distance away. Upon going , there he discovered a woman named Mrs. Wareing. who lives near the Golden Ball, lying in the ditch known as "Pommy Dwyer's." Her body was fast in the mud, and covered with water, but she had managed to keep her head out. Grant at once rescued tee woman from her unplea- Sant and perilous position, and escorted her Part Bay home. It appeared that Mrs. tVareing bad alighted from the St. Helens train at Appleton about eight o'clock, and in the darkness missed her way, and fell into the ditch. When found by Grant she was quite exhausted with her straggles, and would have succumbed in a few minutes. THEFT Of A FISHING SMACK AT ReNCOßN.—Befort. Cap- tain at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Joseph Gillett, 16 years of age, was charged with stealing a fishing smack, valued at £4O, the property ef Wiliam Waterworth. At five o'clock on the previcus afternoon the boat was moored safely at the boat-house pier. Two boars later it was missed, and after five hours' search on tbe river in a small boat, the smack was found straded on a sand bank opposite the Dukes Pier The nets and ballast boards had been thrown overboard. The prisoner, who was on the bank attempted to make ashore, but the water was too eeep, and he had to return. He was captured and given into the custody of Police Clerk Wallace. The priaoner said "W.ll you get the otber mon? HA as bed as me. On the ap- plication of Superiut-mdent Leah, the prisoner was remanded for further inquiries to be made. Tits NORTEWICII Etecrton Riot...-. Eleven men were charged at Northwich on Thursday with rioting mid wil- fully damaging the Conservative central offices on the elec• don day. The magistrate wl.o read the That Act and the magistrates' clerk (both Conservative officials) did not sit. The prosecution was conducted by a late Liberal C isteict agent. Five constables and two Conservative official 9 gave evidence against the prisoners. The defence Was that the conduct of the prisoners did not amount tas rioting, and that the damage was done by other persons. Nine of the defend- ants were bound over to keep the peace and ordered to pay the costs.—A man named Hankey was charged with emelt- ing a constable. Tbe evidence showed that he had deliber- ately and violently bits constable on the head with a stone. Tie magistrates sentenced him to three months hard la sour. lie then threatened revenge on a witneaa (Sergeant 11 and- , ford), and hie sentence was altered to six months' inn-

priaontnent. BRUTALITY AT BALERANIC.—Mary Ellen Langford gam- tnoned her husband, Richard Landford, a labourer, who lives at Halebank. to Widnes Police Court. on Wednesday, on a charge of assaulting ber.—The complainant, who hire marks uf illusage upon her face, said on Saturday afternoon her husband left the house. and did not return until uight. Be said he would learn her for sending to him for three- pence fir lamp oil, and with a blow on the side of the head, knocked her against the wall. He struck her repeatedly on the head and face, and also kicked her. One of her eves was blacked. He had beaten her before, but this was the first time she had summoned him, and she did not want to press the case. She merely wanted him bound over, aod compelled to maintain herself and two children apart from him.—A witness proved the injuries of the woman—the defeedant trade a statetnent to the effect that his wife went into a pubbc-house, and "scandalised" him. When he went borne she took up a carving knife, but be pushed her with his hand, and she fell over the sofa and blaclool her eyes. Her evidence consisted of nothing but "bare-faced lies." During this statement the defendant flourished an ugly looking carving knife about, whilst his wife stamped her foot, Rod cried out in shrill tones that his tale was false. —George Hulmes deposed to seeing the prosecutrix take a glass of whiskey shortly previous to the quarrel.—The Bench hound the defendant over to keep the peace Xpr three months, himself in £2O, and two sureties in £lO. FREE BREAKFASTS FOR SCHOOL CHILDREN AT WIDNES. —A movement is on foot to provide the school children who are suffering, from hanger through tha destitute con- dition of their parents with free breakfasts, and a number of gentlemen have banded themselvee together to carry oat the project. Trade in Widnes is in a most depresaed condi- tion at the present time. There are hundreds of men out of work in consequence, and there is much poverty and die- trees amongst their families. A meeting of gentlemen took place in the Drill Hall on Thursday afternoon to consider what means could be devised to alleviate the distress of the children. The Roy. George Bond, vicar et Farnworth, pre- sided, and there were present the Rove. Father Finegan, 8.. Bordon, R. Yeatman. and D. Davies; Messrs. H. W:Dea- con, T. Sadler, P. Glover. Warren, and S. B. Stringer. Mr. Stringer described tlse means adopted for ascertaining the cases of distress, and said they had about 103 cases, many of a very touching nature, reported. In Waterloo- road School there were 9 cases, at Simm's Cross 44, and at Warrington-road 44.—The Chairman said there were about twelve cases in Farnworth, and these might possibly be extended to twenty. They were chiefly amongst people living in a low neighbourhood. The Rev. Father Finegan said if they were to do anything they must do it in a charitable spirit, and let it extend to all the,poor. In his school there were few cases. tie did however, see a great deal of distress amongst the homes of the poor people, especially amongst the sick and infirm • and he reluctantly joined in any assistance of that Mad' which only reached the school children. If it reached all the destitute, than he would join in the effort. He thought they had selected a rather unfortunate time, for the schools would soon be closed for the Christmas holidays, and coose- quently they would not be able to relieve the distress men- tioned uctil the the 11th of January.—Mr. Stringer saw no reason why their charity should be stopped during the holi- day time.—Mr. Deacon and Mr. Sadler thought the idea a good one.—Eventuelly the Revs. Father Clarke, Father Finegan, Messrs. Deacon, Sadler, and Stringer were appoin- ted a committee to draw up a scheme and submit it to a future meeting. Votes of thanks were accorcld to the chairman and to the teachers at the schools for providing information. It may be mentioned that the School Man- agement Committee of the School Board have power te grant the use of the ocbool kitchens if deemed necessary and advisable.

Mr. 3. GITXST GOENALL, son of Dr. Gomel, has just passed the first examination in chemistry ail physics for the M.B. degree. He is at St. Catherine's College, Cambridge University.

CIikiSTMAS AND NILW Ya.An CARDS.—A large selection of cards for the present season, including the choicest specimens of the lithographic and photographic arts, is pow on view at Mr. John S. Green's, 34, Bridge-street, Warrington. There is also a charming display of the latest novelties in hand-painted cards, water colours, etchings, mirrors, &c., which all readers of the Examiner would do well to inspect.—Advt. A ROYAL COmmissiON ON EDUCATION.—At the instance of the Government Her Majesty is about to issue a Royal Commission to inquire into the workings and results of the Education Acts. The I Commission will, amongst other matters, take into account the subject of over-pressure, and probably also the relations of technical teaching to the ordi- nary day schools of the country. It will be remem- bered that the appointment of this Commission was fore-shadowed by Sir R. Cross in one of his speeches during his election campaign. Tnx Naw'ros ELacTioN.—Captain Seton, of New- ton, has received a letter from Sir Richard Cross, who has been returned in the Conservative in- terest for the Newton Division. dated from the Home Office, Whitehall, in which the right hon. gentleman, after promising to hold a meeting at either Earlestown or Newton before the assembling of Parliament, goes on to say: "I must therefore in the meantime request you to be good enough to thank all those who worked so hard in the good eau.* for their exertion, and to congratulate them upon their success, with an expression on my part of confident reliance upon them for the future, whenever occasion should arise."

PILECEDENCE AT CHCB.CH.--AMCSING LETTER.— A magistrate and alderman of Chester having writ- ten to Sir John Bennett regarding the order of pre- cedence between magistrates and aldermen in municipal processions at church attendance, has received the following reply Cheapside, Dec. 14. —Dear re church processions. On most great occasions, I fear, we are all out of order when we go to church. There being no law, each member is a law unto himself. It is first come first served. In a place of worship one miserable sinner is as good as another. I don't know that heaven cares a fig which comes first. .It seems right that the greater sinner shoukl have the preference. I should add that there is a strong impression abroad among the ungodly that as the worthy aldermen come and go the devil stands at the porch and counts them.— With pious regards, kc., JOHN BENNETT."

ECROYD A.N.D._YRE FAIR TRADERS.— The Tin:a says :—One of the most sig- nihcant and—with all deference to our lively cor- respondent Mr. Howorth—the most satisfactory results of the general election have been the com- plete discomfiture of the Parliamentary advocates of. Fair Trade. Mr. Ecroyd's defeat is not an isolated phenomena. Mr. James Lowther, who is not even a Pair Trader, but something very like a thorough- going Protectionist, has been defeated in Lincoln- shire. Mr. Sampson Lloyd has failed in Warwick- shire. Salisbury has rejected Mr. Coleridge Kennard; Mr. Harris has failed to persuade the electors of Devonshire that they would gain by the imposition. of a duty on flour, and Mr. Hammond, who wooed the electors of Newcastle on a Pair Trade programme, has been beaten by a large majority in spite of the support which the friends of Mr. Cowen gave him. In Lancashire the cry of Fair Trade may have turned the balance in a few constituencies. But in the rural districts the fear of the dear loaf has been fatal to Conservative candidates in all directions.

A Tony lirrrnx. The ladies of the Primrose League have made themselves very conspicuous during the recent elections. Here's a story of the 1 doings of one of them, taken from the Sheffield pendent :—Mrs Heathcote, one of the ladies of the Primrose League. and wife of the candidate for the North-West Staffordshire, was canvassing the other

day somewhere in the Halmerend and Andley min- ing district, when she went into the cottage of a miner. The miner's cat had only a day or two be- fore given birth to a line litter of kittens. Mrs lleathcote, seeking for a good cue to commence her canvassing, exclaimed, "Oh, what beautiful it- tens! I suppose they are all Tories." "Oh, yes V replied the collier's wife. "Then I hope you will give me one of the pretty little things. Can it see?" "No, it cannot see yet," answered the woman, smiling. "Then," said Mrs Heathcote, graciously. I will call for it when it has opened • its eyes." A short time afterwards Mrs Ileathcote again appeared at the cottage, and gushingly ex- claimed, "Oh, where is my pretty little puss? Give it to me, for I want to show it to the Captain. Let me see, you said it was a Tory." " Yes ! It was a Tory when you were here last, but then it could not see, but now it has opened its eyes it's a Liberal."

TRII TIIRRR ACR-RS AND A. Cow: TORY MIS- RBPRMSBNYATION.—The following correspondence has passed between a Newton-le-Willows elector and Mr. Chamberlain respecting the agricultural vote, and the three acres and a cow :—" Newton-le- Willows, Dec. 14, 1885 —Dear Sir,—Permit me as a Lancashire elector to congratulate you and the Liberal party on the glorious victories won in the agricultural counties—places in which Toryism has hitherto reigned supreme. From a just and Liberal standpoint, the reason is not far too seek, for the labourer has at last received his political freedom, thanks to the gallant efforts of yourself and colleagues. I find, however, many Tories are put- ting an entirely different construction on this question, and in this district they openly affirm that the labourer has been induced to support the Liberals under the promise of the 'three acres and a cow.' Pressed for an authority for this statement, they reply that you yourself made the promise in one of your public speeches. Ido not for one moment believe this charge—viz., promising three acres and a cow for nothing—can be proved,' and I am unable to trace any suoh .promise in the copies of yew speeches which I have by me. Both yourself and the agriculturist should be freed from the stigma, and perhaps you will not be unwilling to favour me with an authentic reply for my political oppo- nents.—Apologising for troubling you, I remain yours most respectfully, ----. The Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain, M.P."—[Reply.l--" Mghbury, :%foor Green, Birmingham, Dec. 15, 1885. Sir,—Mr. Chamberlain desires me to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 14th inst., and to say that if you will ask those who make the assertion you mention to refer you to the speech in which any such pro- mise was made, you will find that, as usual. the Tory statement is a misrepresentation.—l am, yours truly, (Signed) W. WOODINGEL" THE REY. CA.NON CARE AND CONVOCATION.— On Friday, the Venerable Archdeacon Bardsley held a court in St. Luke's Church, Liverpool, for the nomination and election of two proctors out of the clergy within the Archdeaconry of Warrington, to sit in the Convocation of York. Amongst the clergy present were :—Revs. J. C. Pigot, W. Flaherty, U. A. WNaghten, J. Barnacle. H. S. Bolton, W. J. Melville (Downall Green), H. Siddall (Ashton), T. R. Matthews (Earlestown), £H. Kearney (Hay- dock), J. Whitley (Wargmve), and 11. Monk (New- ton).—Archdeacon Bardsley asked the clergy to nominate those whom they desired should repre- sent them in Convocation.—Rev. W. J. Melville said he had much pleasure in moving there-election of the Rev. Dr. Carr, vicar of St. Helens, and hon. canon of (nester, whe was one of their veteran proctors, but who, he understood. was to be opposed bv reason of hie age and a recent illness. He ap- pealed to the clergy present that Dr. Carr was, by reason of his past services, his matured experience, his restored health, and his willingness again to serve in Convocation, entitled to the honour of re- election. He had for twenty-seven years out of forty years spent in the ministry worked hard in this diocese; he had never missed a single attend- ance at Convocation since his election some years ago, and he had tried to be fair on all questions which had arisen. The Rey. E. P. llodgins seconded the motion, and, after endorsing the ob- servations of a preceding speaker, referred to Dr. Carr as a most conscientious and indefatigable clergyman. Finding his health failing him, Dr. Carr had placed his resignation in the hands of the Bishop,sbut he had withdrawn his resignation upon his health being restored.—The Rev. Canon Warr, Rev. J. W. Diggle, and the Rev. Canon Penrhvn were also nominated. On the vote being taken the Revs. Canons Warr and Carr were elected proctors by 48 and 2.8 votes respectively. The Rev. Canon. Penrhyn received 25 votes, and the Rev. J. W. Diggle 19. A poll was then demanded, and will be held at. noon on Friday next. (For remainder of Local News sec page. 8.)

WARRINGTON SAVINGS BANK.

The trustees and managers of this bank held their CBth annual meeting at the Bank in Buttermarket-street, on 'Tuesday morning. Major Pickcnere presided, and there were also present Mr. William Long (vice-chairman), the Revs. John Yonge and A. Keuworthy, the Mayor (Alder- man Harrison), and Messrs. F. Monks, Thomas Jolley, C. J. Holmes', Joseph Davies, Samuel Rigby, Win. Derby- shire, S. M. Webster, John Hatton, D. W. Finney, livery Roberts. Thomas Whittle, Charles Broadbent, J. 11. Young, F. W. Monks, Thomas Betide. and J. E. Davies (actuary). THE Bost:cuss or THE Yreart.—The report of the Com- mittee of Management for the past financial year was read. In it was stated that the total funds amounted to £292,145 2s 4d. The tatal amount due to depoeitors was £290,039 Ss Cri, leaving a surplus of £2,105 13s 10d. £7,618 48 3d interest, and £B3 34 61 dividends on stock had been credited to depositors, and the total amount due:to them gave an in- crease for the year of £5,964 Is 41. 774 new accounts bad been opened. and 590 closed, showing an increase for-the year of 184. The total number of depositors was 9,470. The committee again pointed out to depositors who would have more to deposit than £3O a year, and £l5O in the whole, that they may invest through the bank £lOO a year, or any smaller amount not less than £lO, in the purchase of Government stock, azd the bank receives and credits their accounts with their half yearly dividends. The number of investors in stock is gradually increas-1 lug, and the stock register shows a balance of £3,815 of £3 per cent coneuls held by depositors. The increasing number of depositors, and the grow- in of the institution necessitated an extension of hours the bank should be open for business Over one thousand more transactions than last year were recorded, and the committee contilently hoped that the in- crease would continue.—Tire MAYOR proposed—" That the statement of the ueomints prepared by the actuary, and ex- amintd by the accountant, be approved, and one copy of the accennt as directed to be tranemitted to the National Debt. Commissioners, and the duplicate to be publicly affixed in the Savings Bank." It must be gratifying to find that there was an increase in the number of the RC- coucts and in the amount deposited.—Mr. Long seconded the motion. He said tbe work of the bank kad always gone on smoothly and well. They would like to Bee tbe re- turns larger and showing greater vitality, but they were quite agreed that the reason they were not so was the de. I premien or bade and the depressed condition of agricul- ture. They hoped to see a return of the business as the trade of the country improved. (Hear, bear.)—The motion was carried. e

RIGBY proposed "That the report of the Committee of Management is ap- proved, and that this meeting acknowledges the valuable services rendered to the institution by the gentlemen acting on the committee daring the past year, and tenders its beet thanks to them." Tke committee, he said, most assidu- ou lv attended to their duties, and the hitereet and well being of the bank had always been their first charge. ANNUAL GENERAL MEETING. On Thursday morning, the annual general meeting cf the members of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society was held at Ors Lien Hotel, Warrington, "to receive report of council and balance sheet, elect council and efficers, fix dates of next year's e how, select division of society in which the show of 1887 shall be held, revise rules and prizes, and transact any other business." The chair was taken by Lord Egerton of Team], and amongst the large number present were Lrd Wirmar- leigb, Messrs. G. C. Hale. T. Fair, J. W. Fair, J. T. Smith, W. Scetson, J. Southern, J. Warburton, W. Derby- shire, W. Longton, R. Webster, J. Halsall, T. Fig- chett, ctc.

The Rev. JOHN YONGE moved: That the names of the officers and their sureties as read by the Actuary be hereby approved, and that two trustees and three managers sign the certificate to be transmitted to the National Debt Office."—Mr. D. W. FINNThi .sec.nded the motion, and said many congratulations had been expressed that morning npon the success of the institution, and he thought they were will deserved. There was one feature to which be should like to be allowed to refer. It was a gratifying one as showing the popularity of the savings bans in Warring- ton. They had on the one band a great amount of money transferred from the Poet Office Savings Bank to their own hank, and people were so satisfied with the conduct of this institution that on the other band no money bad been transferred to the Post Office. div.head: DASTARDLY OUTRAGE ON RUNCORN
div.p: DASTARDLY OUTRAGE ON RUNCORN

- - BRIDGE. An outrage of a most dastardly character was per- petrated on Runcorn Bridge on Saturday night. The victim in Edward Hill, insurance agent and landlord of the Friendship Tavern, Fryer-street, Runcorn; and the circumstances show that the attack was pre. meditated, and possibly intended to have a fatal ter- mination. About seven o'clock Hill was in the Cen- tral, Hotel, Widnes, where the recent Northwich election formed the subject of discussion between him self and Dr. O'Keeffe and a man named Campbell, who lives at 29, Milton-street, Widnes. Shortly afterwards he left, and walked through Widnes and on to the Bridge with John Jones newsagent, Ash- bridge-street, whom he ha 4 overtaken on the way. Upon reaching the girder nearest the Cheshire side of 1 the river, they heard the footsteps of two men walk- ing at a quick pace behind them. Jones stopped aside to permit them to pass, when one of the men struck Hill on the back of the he3d with some weapon he carried. Turning to face his assailants. Hill was then felled to the ground by a fearful blow on the forehead dealt by the second man, and a struggle ensued, during which the men kicked Hill and Jones cried "Murder, murder," in a voice that I was heard a considerable distance way. The men, I Jones alleges, attempted to throw Hill over the railings into the river beneath, but hear- ing the sound of advancing footsteps they ran off in the direction of Widnee. Hill, stunned and bleeding las he was managed to walk home with the aid of i Jones, and on the way lodged a complaint with Lam- bert, the ticket collector, and informed Sergeant Eger- ton of the brutal attack to Which he had been sub- ject. He was shortly afterwards seen by Dr. Man- gin, who found that he had astained a very serious contused wound on the right temple, and another on the back of the head, his condition from the shock and Iloss of blood giving grave Cause for alarm. He was c mfined to bed for several days. Jones states that the weapons used by the men ware iron bars' and that they had provided against identification by hav- ing their faces masked or blackened. It is conjec- tured that, this cowardly ou•rage is the sequence to Hill's action at the recent Northwich election. Hill is president of the local branch of the Irish National League, end as Mr. Parnell nor his lieutenants for- warded any specific instructions an to how their fellow-countryroeu were to vote in Runcorn and dis- trict. Hill decided, with the concurrence of the priest, the Rev. l'other renuelley, to follow his own political predilections. He gave his adhesion to Mr. Brunner's cause, and it is believed influencedmt least nine-tenths of hie compatricto to follow his lead. His action was , displeasing to some of his friends, in Runcorn. and in Widnes, where he made no secret of his opinion, he was regarded with considerable disfavour. Hence it is Hill's, and the generally accepted idea, that this brutal conduct is the result.

LONDON MISSIONARY SOCIETY. MEETING IN WYCLIFF CHURCH. On Sunday sermons were preached in Wycliffe Congre- gational Church, Warrington, by the Rev. Yonge, in the ' morning, and the Rev. E. IL Stribling, misaionary from Madagascar, in the evening, and oolleetions roads in aid of the London Missionary Society. There were good congre- gations. On Monday evening a tea was held in Wycliffe Hall, for which tables were given by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, Mesdames Armitage, Yonge, Frank Roberts, Tunstall, Wallington, Henry Roberta, Richard Hebert', Walker, Barker, Legge, John Tunstall, Dignum, Garland, Poole, Percival, Ceutts, Birtles, Haynes, Hodgkineoti, Pearson, Plumpton Westgarth, Haynes, Gso. Wallington, Ed. Wel- lington, Renwick, Conley, H. Rathtxme, A. RathOone, Smith, Hodgine, Bouchier, Owen, Clay, W. Whitler, W. Gaskall, Travis; and Mies Garner. After tea a meeting was held in the chapel, the ohair beieg taken by Mr. Z. 'Armitage, J.P. There was a moderate attandance.—The CHAIRMAN *ailed upon the Rev. J. longs to make a state- ment as to what had been done locally in counection with the society. The Rev. J. Yorrou said he wished, and he was sure they all wished, that the statement he had to make was of greater and better things than it happened to be. They re- membered with some regret that at a time not so very long ago Wycliffe Church and Sunday School was accustomed to send to the London Missionary Society a respectable sum of money every year. The Missionary Society lost, at any rate in Warrington. a very valuable friend in Mr. Mur- ray, but the London Missonary Society bad not lost him, I because Mr. Murray was doing in hie Sunday School at Bel- fast precisely what he did in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) He was encouraging the echolers there to give just as he en- couraged those at Wycliffe to give. They bad, however, lost his generous inspiration and example, but their Sunday School had not altogether lost interest in the Missionary Society, and this year he thought there would be something like £25 to go from the Sunday School to the society. (Ap- plause.) Their cengregationel collections were not as mag- nificent as the; ought to be by a very long way, but as twelve months ago they collected between LH and £l7, he was glad to say the collections on the previous day were just a little bit more—he thought about 18 guineas, more or less. They had also had contributed for the purpose of providing the tea that evening between £8 and £lo—(hear, hear)—and he supposed after paying all expenses they would be able to send up £lO or MI as the result of the. tea. Mr. Yonge also mentioned that he had ieceived a sub- scription of a guinea from a gentleman who did not will his name to be mentioned, and he intimated that he would be willing to receive any number of guineas, either anony- mously or otherwise. (Hear, hear.) He thought that alto- gether they would be able to send a few more pounds this year to the London Missionary Society in excess of what they did last year, and he hoped that before very long they should regain the positien they formerly held as con- tributors to that noble institution. (Hear, bear, and ap- plause.) The CHAIRMAN, haying expressed his regret at the smell attendance, said he could not conceive bow it was that men who professed to have an interest in the gospel of Christ could withhold that interest from the spreading of that gospel not only at home but in foreign countries Arguments were sometimes used to the effect that they had no right to send their strength out into foreign countries to the neglect of the work at home. That war perfectly true, but they were not called upon to neglect the work at home. It was also equally true that they had on right to spend all their strength at home to the exclusion of other work that ought to be done all over the face of the earth. He thought the argument was as good on one side as the other. (Hear, hear.) He thought that when two gentlemen came as it were from the ends of the earth to address them on their missionary labours the very least they could do was to give them an audience large enough to show their interest in such matters. He wished it had been in their power to influence their friends to come there and hear the statements that were to be made and help them in spreading an interest in that great cause. Com- plaints were sometimes made about the expense of carry-

log on missionary operations, but he vatitnred to say that a , little examination would convince anybody that they could not conduct operations over the face of the earth, as was done by the London Missionary Society, without consider- , able expense for administrative purposes. (Hear, hear, and applause.) . The Bev. W. Lag (missionary from Travancore. South India) said that the published report of the London Mis- sionary Society was full of ietareet. There was one page . of statistics in the report published this year which chal- lenged attention and deserved the interest of every christian man and woman. The Society this year published its 91st . annual report, and it might possibly help them to remember the following figures if they bore that fact in mind. They ' , had now as a body connected with them the large number of 91,000 church membere and although that was only a small portion of the fruit Of the work of the Society, he thought it was a very noble result, and show-d the very great blessing that had rested on the labours of the mission- aries of the Society. (Hear, hear.) • 'I bey could count in Africa, Chins. India, Madagascar. and other placer, the large number of 91,000 oemmunicants or choreh members, and , In addition to them they had upward. of 325,000 persons I connected orritet their congregations who had given up ' idolatry, in some places demonology and different forms of false religion, and who were now worshippers of the same saviour and the same God. (Applause.) tie himself had laboured in a native kingdom in India ruled over by a native , prime,. It might interest them to knew that something like a third of India in its geographical extent was still ruled over by native prince., and about 60000.000 or 65.000,000 people were still governed by their own princes. The j rulers of Trneancere are amongst the most intelligent and I the cultiveted netive princes of India, and he had been very mach intereeted to tind a native king who knew English I literature, art, and politits, and who was able to offer an in- talligent oninion upon almost every subject it was possible I to speak about. At a nat-ive durber he heard a native . geutlernan read prayers in which be invoked the bles-ines of Almighty God upon the ceremony in which they were ' about to engage, but he had euly been a little while in the country when be foiled that the idea any heathen had of God was sadly different from the idea a cbris- tian had. After be had been in the country two or three months there was another ceremony to which no , European, wee invited to attend. The Prince and leading I men went down in procession to the sea taking the idol I Vishnu with them, which they dipped in the sea, and they I brought it bock, re-placed it in the temple to be worshipped as a god for another six months. Their idols were the incar• nation of all that was cruel, licentious, and abominable in human experience, and their worship was of such a nature , that ineteed of being rendered batter and purer thereby they I , were more and more degraded. He thought it ought to be I I known that just as it was in Corinth of old so was it to-day in India. Tne servers and handmaidens of the temples were ; the fallen women of India, wbo had their homes in the tern- plea, PO that those places which should minister to all that is highest and bent in our aspirations only ministered to that , which was moet licentious and most degrading and corrupt. I Of the converts to Christianity they had made in India, I many were demon-worshippers, and others were idolaters. I They were now gathering tbem into congregations, some I large and some small; they worshipped in chapels built by theineelyee, and their numbers were increasing year by year. Having referred to the willingness of those Indian eeaverts to contribute towards the provision of their own means of worship Mr. Lee gave an interesting biograoh cal account of several individual converts who were regarded as typical of the rest. Be concluded by making an apped for support on behalf of the London Missionary Society. They were, he said, £ll,OOO bebindhand, and they needed an' increase of .615.000 per annum if they were to suocessfullY contiene even the work they were at present engard in. (Hear, bedir, and applause.)

The Rev E. 11. STRIBLING, missionary from Madagascar, next gave an interesting acconnt of missionary work L that island, in the course of which he sang two Malagasy limas In an excellent manner. Referring to Mr. Dignatn, a War- rington gentleman now engaged in missionary work, he said that this proved that they in Warrington( had the interest et that great cork at heart.. (Hear, hear.) The island of Madagascar, he explained, was fear times the size of Eng- land and Wales, though it had only a population of (oar millions, less than the population of London alone. The causes which had brought about the depopulation of the island were beathoniesm, slavery, war, infanticide, and a ' want of medical knowledge amongst the inhabitants. He thought that if their forefathers had not sent ntissienaries to I Madagascar the country would have been almost depopu- lated by this time. The slave trade had now been stopped, and although prior to the advent of the missionaries there had I been constant wars for many years there bad been peace until the oatbreak of the wretched French war two and a half years ago. (Hear, hear.) Infanticide still prevailed. in I the island, hut that and superstition of every kind was hying I removed by means of the echoele that had been founded. In connection with the London Missionary Soc ety and the Societies of the Friends and Norwegians theee were 130,795 meholare taught in 1.124 echoole. (Applause.) Of these I scholars 40,000 peened in reading last year, their education I being very much like that of the Hoard schools they had in England. (Hear, hear.) There were 60,000 church mem. hers in Madagascar, and in the district in which he had laboured there were 1,700. In conclusion he referred to several incidents in connection with the war the French were waging with the Slalagare, and to tbe noble be- haviour of the latter towards Europeans living in their coon try. At the conclusion a hearty vote of thanks was accorded bo Mr. Lee and Mr. Stribling, on the motion et the CRATE- Kara.

-LOCAL NEWS. ' I (Continued from page 1) • "Church and State from the time of the Reformation" wee the title of a paper read before the members of All &loth Debating Society on Monday night by the Bev. I.

M. Ammon. PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, RUIROORIL— The members had their fortnightly entertaiemeot on Thurs. day night in Regent-street Schoolroom. Mr. Thomas Poole presided, and there was a fair attendance. WIDNES NATIONAL Souoots.—With the object of rais- ing funds to repsir the exterior of Waterloo-road schwas, a concert was given there on Thursday nign,. Thzr.! was only a poor attendance, and the Rey. A. P. Hamilton Wil- son presided. A tong but interesting programme Of songs, instrumental selections, and readings was gone through in capital style. CHILDREN'S PANTOMIME AT, licscome A crowded audience assembled in Runcorn National Scuool on Thursday evening to witness the pantomime " Puss in Boots" The nanierous characters were taken by children of the Parish Chureb Sunday School, and the airmrable manner lo which they went ttirougu the petformance merits the warmest praise. The scenes were very effective, the Ocruses and songs were sung In capital style ash the en- tire entertainment was very enjoyable. The prlncleal char- acter') were :—Puss (afterwarcs Lord Carabas), Charles Clarke; Florinet, the millets) son, John Hampson ; King, Edward Harrington ' • First Lord of the Court, Arthur Houghton ; Second ditto, Henry Coward,: Ogre, Henry Clarke; Herald, Harold Davies ; Rick, the eprite. Ttianyie Williarnean . • Queen, Annie M. es ; Princess, Any Hancock; Ladies-in-Waiting, Lizzie Coward, Clara Withington. Flo- rence Gorst ; Fairy, Clara Hampson. A tOpciil sons com- posed for the occasion was the cause of considerable amuse- ment. THE SHIP CANAL Wonics.—On Monday morning about 200 navvies commenced the work of connect- ing the new trench excavated by the Bridgewater Navigation Company between .Mode Wheel and Throstle Nest with the river Irwell. When the Ship Canal Bill was passed in July, this work was stopped. It is said the work is .now being com- pleted prior to the 'property of the Navigation Com- pany being transferred, to the Ship Canal Com- pany. The water in the Irwell was turned off on Mor.day to allow of the connecting of the new arm with the upper and lower portions of the I river, and the repairs of the weir at Mode Wheel. A large number of people visited the works during the day. A ST. HELENS DIVORCE SUIT.—In the Divorce Division, on Wednesday, *Mr. Justice Butt bad be- fore him the case of Tilley, v. Tilley. The petition was that of Mrs. Elizabeth Tilley for a divorce by 'reason of the cruelty, desertion, and adultery of her husband, Mr. James Henry Tilley, a butcher, of Liverpool-road, St. Helens. There was no defence. The parties were married on the Ist of October, 1878, at St. Thomas's Church, St. Helens, and there was one child subsequently born. Upon several oc- casions he assaelted her, and had threatened to kill her ; in addition to which he falsely 'aceused her of improper conduct with a policeman. Owing to his violence `she was obliged to leave. There was no defence, and the case being established the learned judge granted a decree nisi with costs. RUNCORN PATENTEES.—Messrs. S. Crosby and Sons, Top Locks, Runcorn, have patented and just registered tjle trade mark of a new food for calves. The first distinguishing name selected ,by the firm was " Lactine," but this was held to be an infringe- ment of that used by a Lancashire manufacturer. " Cremor " was substituted. A trial resulted before. the Controller of the Patent Office, and a German firm was given it verdict that they had a prior right tO that name. At last Messrs. Crosby have suc- ceeded in obtaining the title " Cremoid " for their special manufacture with a suitable trade mark, and the farmers.of Cheshire and adjoining counties, who are deeply interested in the important subject of rearing calves, will hail with pleasure any pro- duction likely to be of benefit. It is claimed that Cremoid is the purest, healthiest, and most nutri- tious milk substitute for calves ever mauufac- tured. THE *HEAT TOY DA.RLIAMENT.—Ottr advertisi columns to-day contain an announcement of the opening of the "Grand International and Antedi- luvian Bazaar and Toy Fair," at Compton House, Liverpool, the Fell-known establishment of Messrs. Watts and Co. The enterprise of Messrs. Watts and Co. is of a peculiarly interesting character, and their advertisement will amply repay perusal. Following the announcement that" The Grotto will throw open its magic portals at ten o'clock prompt," we are Informed that a Great Toy 'Parliament" will be held, and a "Proclamation" is issued, stating that the "Patriarch Noah" has been appointed Prime Minister. "The Grotto "is explained as "sacred to magic and mystery," and there are "spectral illu- sions, dazzling apparitions, images of imagination, marvellous effects of Fairy Queen witchery and castles in, the air, with gleaming turrets." There are toys from every nation under the sun, and it is stated there are "large toys, for ye goode girles and boyes," in the "New Parliament under a Coalition Ministry." The political allasions are very appro- priate,while the" Startling revelations, spiritualistic manifestations, and facts about the deluge" are exceedingly interesting. A DISPUTED PROMISSORY NoTE.—At the Wigan County Court orl Wednesday an action was brought by John Rogerson, tailor, Wigan. against William Urquhart, merchant, tailor, Newton-le-Willows, to recover £l2 3s 3d, the amount of a promissory note given bjr the defendant and endorsed to the plaintiff.—Mr. Ackerley appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A, Browne, of Warrington, for the defen- dant.—lt seems that the note was payable at the Manchester and County Bank, Wigan, on the sth November last, and the plaintiff presented the note there on the 7th • November, when it was dis- honoured, hence the present action.—For tile de- fence Mr. Browne stated that his client, the defen- dant, tendered the amount of the note at the Manchester and County,, Bank, Wigan, on the day when it became due, but as the ,note had not been presented the bank refused to accept the money. Mr. Browne now contended that the defendant had done all that was required of him, and that the plaintiff was not entitled to re- cover because he had failed to present the note on the date it became due.—Mr. Ackerley, in reply, contended that this being a- general promise to pay and not payable at the Ms.nchester and County Bank only, presentment was not necessary, but that the defendant was bound either to have a fund in the bank ready to meet the amount' of the note when presented or tender the amount to the plain- tiff personally.--His Hortottr, after perusing the report of a case cited by Mr. Ackerley, said there 'must be judgment for the plaintiff for the amount claimed and costs.

FAT STOCK Sates.—On Tuesday Messrs. Mainwaring and I and Co. held their usual sale of fat stock at the Queen's Head Hotel, Frodsham, where there was an excellent show of cattle which found ready purchasers at good prices, the whole of the stock being cleared off. There was a large at- tendance of buyers. A sale was also held on the same day at the Bear's Paw Hotel, Frodsham, by Messrs. Pickering and Nightingale, of Chester. ACCIDENT TO Ma. THOMAS RIG.—On Monday, Mr. Thomas Rigby, the esteemed secret try of tin ROTal Man- ' cheater, Liverpool, and North-Lancashire Agricultural Society. was attemptiog to get into a train at Fro& sham, not being aware that it was in motion, when his foot slipped and he fell between the carriage and the platform. lie was at once dragged from his perilous position by some friends who were, fortunately, near him at the time, thought he was much Arkken and loafed, necessitating confinement to his room for several days. INFANTS' CONCEET.—A concert was given by the chil- dren attending the Infant School, Frodsharn, in the Town Hall, on Monday evening, when the room was crowded and the efforts of the little folks were very successful and duly appreciated by the audience. A temperance meeting was afterwards held, when addresses were given ry the Rev. H. B. }nogg, M.A., vicar of Frodskam, and the Rev. W. Cogs- well, M.A., vicar of St. Oswald's, Chester. A vote .of thanks was accorded to Miss Platt and assistants for the efficient manner in which the children 'had been trained for the concercAnti a vote of thanks was also given to the •Rev. W. Cogswell for his interesting address.

TION, A bazaar and industrial exhibition' WAS commenced in Camden Wesleyan School on Wednesday afternoon. The room presented a very bright and • pleasing appearance. Festoons depended in graceful curves from the ceiling, and holly and ivy was tastefully disposed on the walls. Upon the stalls were a choice and varied amortment of articles with a wealth of bright colour. At the to end of the build- ing was a handsome fir tree beautifully " frosted." with an admirably arranged base while in the centre of the room was a fountain from Heath Hours, A rocky foundation ,• norm.° " with ivy, and the musical ripple of th fal- ling water gave ia v.::: eateral and picturesque effect. Most in' obj cm were the beautiful models of steam- ' boats, exhibited by tne kindness of Messrs. Laird Bros., and the Welsh Coast Steamboat Co., and they attracted considerable attention. A model sa.ling yacht bown lby Mr. williara Tittle, completed the embellishments of the building. Toe object of the bazaar was to raise £125 with which to liquidate a nutnber of small debtsiocerred in carrying on the work of school and chapel, and the good audience that assembled at the opening ceremony was an indicstion of the istereat Liken in the project. Amongst those present were the Rev G Wood, T Hackett, A P W at- son , Messrs P Speakman, J Simpson, T Simister, S C Heckert', T Bowe, J Timperley, J Havenscroft, H dtandle, WJ Shore, G Yarwood, r Cooke, J W Woodland. and A Harrison and J Nancellis (secretaries to the bazaar); Mrs Speaktnao, Mrs Shaw, Mrs T Haztehurst, Mrs Wood, Mrs Hackett, Mrs Watson, Mrs Bellamy. Mrs W J Shore, Mrs Randle, and Mrs Handley. The Rev 0 Wood con- ducted the proceedings, mad introduced Mr P Speaktnen, of "the Mount." tiigner Runcorn, to perform the opening ceremony. Mr. Speakman said the great object th. y had in view was to make money, and the useful purpose to which that mousy vonitt be pet Would be known to everybody who haat lived in Runcorn for the last 20 years, and observed the work an- compltshed at Camden School. (Idenr,hear.) He referred -to his early associations with the school, remarking that the name of Hezleburst would ever be associated with its foundation. '.Tee departure bf Mr 0 S Hazlehurst was a great loss to the school, but God in his providence had raised up others to carry on the work, and difficulties had been met through the beneficence of their friends from time to time. But still there was always oil wanted for the machinery if it were to be kept reeving smoothly, and money was the oil that was required to keep that beautiful school and sanctuary at work. It was for that purpose they ware met that slay. There were in c(.n. nection with Camden Sunday School a noble band of volunteers. (Hear, hear.) It was encour- aging to see the teachers attending Sabbath after Sabbath and year after year. and now they had arraneed this bazaar and exhibition so that !hone who took no part In the actual work of the Sunday school should have an opportunity of showing their appreciation of what had been I accomplished. (Applause.) After alluding to bazaars and to the necessity of unity in all undertakings, Mr. Speakman declared the bazaar open. The fair saleswomen then commenced business. There i were four stalls laden with a large variety of things, the • product principally of the teachers' deft fingers, and they were presided over by Misses Wood, Handley, Chadwick, Dobsou, Speakman, Shaw, Harrison, E. Wood, Tiroperley, Hussey, Liverley, l. Ford, Neild, Riley, and Davies. Amongst the articles it is worthy of mention that there were two beautiful oil paintings, the work and gift of Mr. H. Fitton, and an amusing design in terracotta was contributed by Mr. Andrew Matthews, Mr. S. C. Beckett gave a bracket% decorated with macrame work, the result uf his own Miss James had a stall of Confectionery, and Mr. G. Bellamy offered for sale a quantity of books and fancy articles A "toy stall" was in charge of Miss Peacock and bliss Marsh Hanging upon the waifs for sale were three paintings in oil, I which attracted much attention. The artist was Mr. Jos. I Fearneet, a boatman, and the views taken from nature did him great credit. A feature of the bazaar was the indus- trial stall. The school committee bad offered privm to the scholars for the beat productions in wool work, fret work. drawing, dic., and the results of the industry of the prize winners were exhibited, a list of which is given below. In the evening a variety of entertainments were provided. *•Thatirna, the Parisian mystery," was a realistic represen- tation' of a lady without body, and dial Mr. Coventry and Mr. J. A. Smith, who carried out the idea much credit. Messrs. Fitton and Ainsworth had arrrnild an excellent concert, and the" living wax work" of Mr. J. H. Harrison ' was an unfailing source of amusement. On Thursday evening the prrzes awarded to the competi- tors in the industrial exhibition were distributed by Mrs Shaw, of the Highlands, in the presence of a large assembly. Mr S C Beckett presided, and in introducing Mrs Shea, said the result of the competition was eminently satisfac- tory. The judges of the girls' work were Mrs Soulby, Miss Peacock, Mile Ellis. and Miss Cook ; and of the boys' work Mr Fitton and Mr Boots. Some .of the work was very meritorious, and the general result would warrant them in renewing the industrial competition another year. (Applause.) Mrs Shaw then distributed the prizes as follows :—Class (under. 12 years of age), Lord's prayer : Ist, Beatrice 1 Wood ; 2nd, Ernest A Ward. flemrned handkerchief : Lizzie Fitton ; 2nd, Florence Wood. Six yards of crotchet edging: Ist, Florence Marsh ; 2nd, Elizabeth Burrows. Knitted garters : let, Annie Rogers; 2nd, Lizzie Fitton. Wool ball :' Ist, Rowland Handle ; 2nd, J Duncalf. Wool cuffs : let, Lottie Fitton ; 2nd, Sarah Gillgrass. Mac- rame work : Ist, Harold Randle. Child's knitted socks: Is', Fanny Dutton ; 2nd, Fanny Dutton. Embroidered mats (extra prize): Lottie Shaw. Tam O'Shanter (extra prize) : Annie Smith. Class B (under 18 years), map of Europe: Ist, Samuel Littler •, 2nd, Charles Ditch- field. Knitted stockings (adults): let, Bertha White ; 2nd. Edith White. Child's frock and piaatore : let, Emma Peacock. Child's flannel skirt and singlet : Ist, Martha Walker. Woollen antimacassar : Annie Rogers (6 years of age.) Pin cushion Ist, Sarah Ellen Tittle. Woollen shawl : Ist, Mary Rogers ; 2nd, Lottie Fitton. Cloud (woollen): Extra prize, Mary Jane Tickle. Extra prizes—Fretwork :John Dutton and Arthur Dattos. Wheel- barrow : John Anderton. On the motion of Mr. Randle, seconded by Mr. Shore, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded it Mrs r-haw.—Mr. Robert Shaw replied on behalf of his wife, and observed that the obj.mt of training little bands to useful and indus- trious habits was a very laudable erne fur the school to aim at, and Mrs Shaw aid himself had great Osamu° in being present and helping on thie occasion. (Applause.) The amount realised up to Thursday night was upwards of £7O.

THE USE OF OIL AT SEA. LECTURE AL' RUNCORN.

Under the tqle of " Oil on trouoled waters," Cautain Le Courtier, of Weston Point, on tllondeY evening delivered a lecture to a good audience ef seafaring and otner poreons in the room of the Runcorn Y.M.C.A. Mr. George Moss oc- cupied the chair... Captain Le Coutier takee great interest is OE subject of the use of oil at sea, and having hart his own life &re-ad in a storm of tbe Florida coast through poutleg oil on the troubled waters. his remerke were listened to with greet interest and intelligence. At the outset he give a brief account of no less • them ten cases which had come under his notice since Januery, 18813, where the em• pleyment of oil had been the means of saving life and pro- perly. Commenting upon the experlmehts made by the Chief Inspector of Life Boats, and dinipproved. Captain f.e Ceutier contended that when a life boat, or any other boat, was going from windward to the rescue of a disabled or wrecked ve-ssel, if oil were poured on the water when in close proximity to the veseel, its influence would be felt by the time the boat had rounded under the lee, and the reecue would be facilitated. if, on the other hand, the rescuers were approaching from leeward, th€u the crew of the die- Wed craft should pour on the oil as it would enable the rescuers to reach them quicker and easier. When a boat had to be lowered in a gale of wind and the veseel sac trove to and stationary, oil might be need to advantage. The use .of oil would, however, be of no avaP when a vessel was "bead- reaching," as it would be continualor sailing away from its iefluence. It was the heavy seas a d the creet3 of the waves that swept the decks and "pooped" a vessel, hut a beg of oil towed astern would avert 'Nat calamity. How often had they read of a crew after abandoning their dis- abled or wrecked vessel being swamped and drowned by the surf on the shore. Oil poured over the stern would have enabled them to land safely as it enabled him to do on the coast of Floride. The most dangerous of all maeceuvres to perform was to round a vessel in a gale of wind and a heavy running sea. With less then a gallon of oil the feat hid been accomplished without shipping any water. Inn conclu- sion the lecturer urged that it should be made compulsory for every vessel to be provided with a jar of oil, say even three gallons, and a canvass bag, to be used in cases of necks- sit. That instructions for its use should he printed on sill kg books, as the method of using life-saving rocket appara- tus ; that they should be printedeand posted up in all our Custom trouser., and on every pillar and post around our docks, and in every ship, cabin, and forecastle. Then if in the burry, bustle, MO confusion of the storm, the captain or officers should forget the Influence of oil on troubled waters, perchance the sailors or cabin boy might remind them.— On the motion of Mr. Davies, seconded by Ceptain Paul, a cordial vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer.

THE ASSESSMENT OF THE BRIDGEWATER, NAVIGATION COMPANY. .

RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT RUNCORN. A meeting of the ratepayars of Runcorn took place in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Monday night, for the purpose of considering a letter received from the Assessment Com- mittee of the Union. relative to the aseessmeat of the pro- perty of the Bridgewater Navigation Company in the town- ship at Runcorn, and to appoint a valuer. Mr. William I:Lindley was voted to the chair, and amongst those present were Messrs. W. Whittaker, R. Shaw, W. Farrell, G. Moon, E. Liaison, J. Bridgewater, J. K. Digges, Littler, O'Leak, 11. Brookes, T. Handley, W. Sutton (assistant overseer), . . .

Mr. Sutton read the letter, which was to the effect that the Assessment Committee desired to know the valuations of each separate property of the Bridgewater Navigation Company in the township. The Chairman said toe overseers were not in a position to give these particulars, because it bad been the custom lo supply the valuations of works direct from the Assessment Committee, far many years past Mr. Linaker having under- taken that work at the request of the committee. It must Pccin to them all that neither Mr. IVhittaker nor himself were aoqoainted with this kind of property, end that it was impossible for them to furnish the ieformation requested. The overseers did not feel justified in incurring the expense necessary to obtain the particulars by a re-valuation unless the rate- payers gave them rower to do so. Mr. Handley gave some very interesting -figures with respect to the Bridgewater Navigation Co.'s prnperty, In 1862 the property had a gross rental of £7,500, and a rateable value of £5,500. In 1863 the valuation was raissd to £9,000 gross and £7,200 rateable, being an increase of £1,700 on the rateable value. This vaivatinn was made by Messrs. Corbett and Baby, who received a fee of £69 16s for their cervices. The Bridge- water Trgstees successfully appealed against this valuation. and it was reduced in 1865 to a rateable valne of £5.477 14s 6d, being a decrease of £1,722 Sc 6d. This involved expense. and the overseers had to pay a bill of costs to Messrs. Nicholson and White of £lO4 3s 411. This valua- tion stood until 1870. In that year it was further reduced. The gross reotal was then presumed to be £5,641 193 8d and the rateable value £4,512 11s 10,1, or a decrease of £965 2s 3d.".1n 1876 the gross value was taken at £6,041 193 8,1 and the rateable at £4,913 11e 9d, or an increase of £4OO 19s 11d. These valuatioss were all done at the expense of the Bancorn Union Assessment Committee, and in 178 he distinctly remembered Mr. H. Linaker made this valuation : —Warehouses, offices, timber yards, etebles, wharfee, and landing places, gross value £4,300, and rateable £4,300, the distinction between gross and rateable being thus wiped out. The canal towing paths, docks, water space, akc.. were put down at £1,500, both gross and rate. able value; beim: a rateable value of the two kinds of property ef £5,800. It was this which the Overseers were asked to divide into various particulars. How was it to be done? As Overseers they could not; must they get a valuer to do it? If they passed a resolution to re-value the property, and appointed a person to perform the work, it would be subject to the consent of the Assessment Commit- tee. If the assessment was increased one-sixth, though the Union bed got the benefit, the cost might be charged upon the township rate, but if the value were not raised to that extent tha common (Mid of the Union would have to bear the expense. Mr. 0. Leak: Are we bound to supply the informa- tion? The Chairman replied that if they refused the assess- ment Committee could do it for them. Mr. Robert Shaw said he believed the proper course fe rake would be to ask the Assessment Committee that there should be a revaluation of all the works and property ii, Ruecorn—(bear, hear)—and that it should be done by some independent person outside the Union altcg,ether. It might be quite true that the property of the Bridgewater Naviga- tion Company ought to be raised, but there were other works in the town which were not, in his opinion, properly asses- sed. That might appear to reflect somewhat upon the Assessment Committee. He could not help it if it did. There Was great depression taking place in large household

TRADES COUNCILS. Sir,----What to do and how to do it must very often be a puzzling queettoo to a Trades Council. Iby no means wish it to be understood that in saving a few words about these representative bodies that I am capable of pointing out clearly the mode of procedure in any given difficulty. It eeems to me that the position is something like this. A Trades Council has hitherto existed for the purpose of as- sisting by advice, and as far as it can, in a pecuniary sense, the members of the various societiee represented. It Inns: be ciear to all that to be able to give advice both sides should be heard. How often is this the cam? In no case is capital represented or even heard in defence, only when it cares to put forth a statement in the public press. In the meantime a strike has resulted and bitter feeling caused between employer and employed. Here is a fair Ichance for aTradee Council to step forward and act as an Arbitration Court. It can only do this if it fully and nom- ' pietely represents labour. Members of a Trades Council, being also members of a Trades Union, should have definite principles before them. Knowing what they are aiming at they should understand that it is only by unanimity of opinion that their object is likely to be gained. In the history of past unionism I find that the nom. ber of hours a man should work has been one of the rough- est questions- to struggle with. The difference between " day work" and •• piece wank " has led to disintegration, and selfishness, where piece work was concerned, leading men to work meal hours. as well as ordinary hours, has re- sulted in a fixed minimum wage, with a fixed maxi- mum amount of work. The evil effect of this will at I once be seen by all who care to look at the question care- fully. The principle involved is one especially for a Trades I Council's consider ition.
ERGES,
CLOT H. Warranted to Wear and always Look Well.

In the preamble to the rules of the Warrington Trades Council, I find the following :—" Our labour is our own c.pital. It behoves us then, to place ourselves in a posi- tion to assert our right to a voice in the divosal of our ltbour." These are brave words, and one wonders how it is to be done if mere unity alone is to be depended upon. Here we have capital on one side and labour on the other ; a dif- ference of opinion arises as to the amount of wage to be paid for a certain class of work. Either the emnloyer can afford to pay what is demanded or be cannot. Who is to judge? Certainly not the workmen, because they haveno data by which to be guided, and quite as certainly not the employer, because that would be altogether too one-sided an arrang.ment. The Federation of Workmen could force an amicah'e and equitable settlement of all disputes, the Trades Council to bathe forcing medium. I read in the rules now before me—" Political discussions also to be excluded, except in cases where they directly affect the interests of the working-classes." The reason why a rule of this kind should be held over a Trades ICouncil, is easy to find. There are workmen who fancy themselves Tories ; hence the possibility of political dis- cussion. But the question may be fairly asked why shank' working-men take sides ? Whig and Tory so far have only represented capital; no bond has hitherto existed be- tween these two aneifahour. What lakour has got she has

become possessed of in sp,te of all political parties, and net in consequence of their love. No political hindrances now exist to the associated action of the people, at the same time no redress of grievances need be expected except by political means. Then a Trades Council should at once become the most powerful political machinery in existence. A Trades Council working as a political body could select and elect such men 0111 V SA were pledged to look after the national welfare. Hitherto 11:1002 beat of Parliament have looked aftter class interests, the re- salt of which we see In a National Clairch forsaken by the rural populations, and our large towns swarming with rookeries.

A People's Party should be formed by the Trades Coun- cil, taking up the question and cirrying out a system of lectures on subjects hearing on the workingman's welfare. Who can deny that Joseph Arch will he better able to deal with questions affecting the agricultural labourer than Lord 11. Betitinck ? And yet there are workmen wno would vote for the lord in preference to the labourer. What matters it to me what Sir G. Greenall calls himself or Mr. W. Cron- field ? They are both rich men, and neither of them likely to vote away their possessions, but if a Trades Council, con• fident in its strength, appeared upon the scene, their ans- wers and their conduct in Parliament would bare to be shaped satisfactorily, or else they must make room for bet- ter men.

Constructive work for a Trades Council abounds; and now that the doors of St. Stephens are being opened wider to admit the labourer and th; miner, we must be prepared to render help to these men. Those who have read the reports of the recent Commis- sion on Education, and the juet issued report of the Royal Commission on Depression of Trade and Industry, must be struck by the repeated references to our want of facilities for imparting Technical Education, and how unfavourably we in Eegland compafe witht the continental cities. Scarcely a man-ifacturer of importance writes or speaks without making reference to our deficiency in this direc- tion.

If I might make a suggestion to the Warrington Trades Connell, it would be this : Appoint a deputation at once to wait upon the Mayor and ask him to call a meeting of representative employers and workmen, and see if some arrangements cannot be made for a few lectures by such men as Mr. Stagg or Mr. Mather, hl P. Those lectures might be made preparatory to rennin?, a committ.e for earring out an educatial programme'that would make it • . on. .
impossible for the intelligent son of a poor man to miss his path in life. .

- I hope what I have said respecting Trades Councils will not only draw attention to their existence, but will induce workingmen to join. Of course, baieving, as I do, that the right of one class of msn to control the actions If another body of men is simple despotism, I must also assert the right or all men te gain a livelihood. To do this without injuring one another, I look for full and complete Federation of hour. I cannot understand why one moo should be ex. pealed to bring up a family wi.h credit to himself and the State on .£1 per week, and another man, no whit better either in brain or muscle, should be able to spend as much on a toy. These are important questions claiming full dis- mission in a thoroughly representative Trades Council. CLIFFORD DIX.

Mr. Joshua Sudwortb, matcher, was returning borne from !Ham, where be bad been on his rounds selling meat. MR. GLADSTONE AND ROME RULE. The "Standard " of Thursday says :—We are in a peel' tion to state that the following are the lines on which Mr. Gladstone on taking ollice will be prepared to deal with the question of Home Rule in Ireland :—fho maintenance of the unity of the empire. the authority of the Crown and the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament,to be aesured, the creation of an Irish Parliament to be entrusted with the entire management cf all legislative and adminietrative affairs, securities being taken for the representation of min' orities, and for an equitable partition of all Imperial charges. One of the guarantees suggested would probablY be the nomination of a certain proportion of the Irish mem. hers by the Crown. Mr. Gladstone telegraphs regarding the "Standard noencement of his views upon Home Rule :—The statement is not as accurate representation of my views, hut is, I pre' mime, a npeculation upon them. It is nor published with my knowledge or authority, nor is any other beyond MY own public declarations. " United Ireland " (Mr. Parnell's paper) saye :—lf it be true that the Tories have resolved to bid nothing higher than a county government scheme, that only implies that I the Tories have reseei- to believe that their opponents Two to bid an Irish Parliament, and have made up their min& that it is upon that ground the conflict in the new Parlia- ment will be fought out. Os Thursday evening the Pall Mall Gazrite gave great prominence to the foliewing:—" Mr. Gladstone has riot I only dreinitely adopted the policy of Home Rule for Re. I land, but the details of his Droposals are now before the public. Mr. Gladstone has issued a par tin l dententi of some of the statements put out in his name, especially of the glosses introduced by one of our contemporaries; but we are in a poeitien nevertheless, to state that the following sins- mary substantially embodies Mr. Gladstone's present Were* Cons on the subject. Summarised in the briefest form they are as follow : "1. A. Parliament in Dublin. having complete control et Irish affaire. "2. The right of veto to be exercised by the Crown On/Y ' upon the advice of an Irish Ministry. "3. The Irish representatives to continue to sit at I Westmimeer for all purposed of Imperial legislation. i "4. The police organisatioa in Ireland to be entire/ ! eder Irish control.' "5. Mr. l'arnell to furnish adquato guarantees for the, protection of the loval minority, and the safeguarding of legitimate landlords"' interests. The Central 71,eas, referring to the above, nays —Tbe Pall Mall' Ga-zette gives currency to a report that Terd Spencer has been efon over to a Home Rule policy, and WO practically convince 1 that no other policy .was possible. Although in the highest circles such preposals are declared to he both premature and inaccurate, it is certain that sell scheme of Home Rule has been drawn up, but that it be such a complete surrender to Irish demands as the P9' Mall Geszatte indicates is scarcely credited. Lord Spate!ar adheres to the opinions he has always expressed, and ha' by no means acquiesced in the Borne Itule proposals wee. Honed, or in any other Home Rule scheme. His LordshiPa On being referred to by the Central News, telegraphed to that agency r—" No scheme of Rome Role for Ireland has fe. ceived my approval.—SPEncee " ANOTHER TELEGRAM FROM MR. CiLADSTONf', The Central News says that though all the versions 0' Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule scheme have been declared 10 accurate, the publication has had the effect of allowing the_ right hon. gentleman to see how such prepoeals would he received if formally issued on his authority. It moreovet forms a tangible basis upon which the Irish party can dill' cuss and formulate their counter scheme. In a tetegretu to the Central News agency on Friday, Mr. Gladstone referring to the desire for more explicit information, says:"... e From my Public declarations at Edinburgh with respect to the Government, you will see I have no communicatlol to make." In this telegram the right hon. gentlernas verts to his West Calder speech. It is therefore eviden: that Mr. Gladstone will not formulate his scheme 0' Home Rule until he is himself in a position t° give effect to it. The idea that Mr. Gcschen will1;:ef brought over to support such a scheme of Home Rule that indicated on Friday, is scouted by those who he?' know the right hon. gentleman. Mr. O'Connor Power, tO an interview with a representative of the Central News at Friday, said—" I approve of the scheme. I have alwaa'n9 been in favour of a similar proemial since I had a seat 10 Parliament." The loyalists of Ireland have begun to 'I,. threatening language, and tbe "Globe" on behalf of t"" Conservative party, declares against the Home Rule Pre' posats.

div.head: LYNN.
div.p: LYNN.

The annual meeting of the Lymin Liberal Associaticn will be held in the Mission Dail, Lymm, on Monday evening, INQUEST. •-•• On Monday Mr. Ridgway, coroner, held an inquest at the Wheat Sheaf Inn, Lyinm, touch- ing the death of William Shufflebottom, rdlar, of Broom. edge. Deceased, who was an earthenware dealer, was ,50. years of age. For the last three months he hal suffered from a cough. but had been able to follow his business up to Friday night last. On Saturday morning be awoke about four o'clock, and complained of something in his throat'. Ile became worse, and died about half-past one o'clock. A Post- mortem examination had been made by Dr. Gallimore, who found that the cause of death was inflammation of the lungs. A verdict to the effect that deceased had died from natural causes was returned.

Ltnan named John Huffy was remanded by the Liver- pool magistrates on Wednesday. charged wan the wilful murder of John Wainwright, at Gannon. At the Central Criminal Court, on Wednesday, a young man, named Het,re Pat, ick, ship's cook, was sentenced to death for the murder of Rachael Bayley at Poplar on the 23rd ult. EARLESTOWN BOWLING Cuter —ln aid of funds of the Earleetown Subscritvion Bowling Club a concert was held in the Co-operative Hall,Earle-street on Saturday even- ing. The attendance was only small, but the proceedings were of an enjoyable character. Mr. Peter Hastie was the principal vocalist, and he was Enthusiastically recalled after each selection. tile first contribution was " The man of war," and as an encore he sang "The little hero." His next selection was "Nil desperandum," and on being re- adied he gave "Over the rolling sea." Mr. S. Swann, of Farlestown, also received a warns welcome, and his songs The heroes" and "Out on the deep; were finely ex- ecuted, the last named being deservedly encored. Miss Bothwell, in her canal excellent stvle, Pang "The lost 33n, and "It was the time of roses.';and she was heartily applauded. As a response she repeated a portion of the last darned piece. The comic selections of Mr. Littler, of Ash- ton (who gave "The Irish girl" and "The boat that brought me over,") and Mr. J. W. Willirms, of Earlestown (who gave "My wife's relations " and selections on the banjo) were greeted with prolonged laughter and en- thusiasm. They were warmly encored on each occasion. A selection ef Lancashire readiags were given by Mr. florridee, who *as awarded with applause; and the pro- ceedings concluded with the National Anthem. I

The District Education-Cm7l;4;e-reported that during the month of Vovember there were 117 applications for tees, which were recommended to be paid in 103 cases. 229 persons appeared before the committee for contravention of the Education Act, and 40 persons were prosecuted and convicted.—Tbe report was adopted on the motion of Father Clarke.

The School Management Committee recommended that the salaries of a flambe' of teachers in each school be in- creased according to the rules of the Beard. div.head: THIS SCHOOLMASTER AND THE ELECTION.
div.p: THIS SCHOOLMASTER AND THE ELECTION.
Father Clarke said he understood that recent'y a head teacher was absent without leave trona school and otherwise employed, and asked for an explanation. - • -

Father 'Finegan replied that be supposed the reference I was to Mr. Hunter, of Warrington-road school, who was employed ae a poll clerk at the election. He was asked the day previous whether or not there would be holidays at I Warrington-road school. He replied that he kept his I school open and saw no reason why the teachers and scholars of Warriositon-road school should have r holiday. Mr. Hunter, nevertheless, absented himself.—The Chairman remarkou that Mr. Showau and Kr. rinosldy were engaged as poll clerks, but their schools were closed, and he saw no impropriety in their so acting. —Father Finegan : Nor I. I consider that it was not right for Mr. Hunter to be absent himself from school without leave.—The Chairman : Certainly not. I think the Committee ought to take it up. Mr. Danby, in response to Father Finegan, said the matter was brought before the School Management Committee, mad he ex- plained that the returning officer required a polling clerk, and he recommended Mr. Hunter. Ile gave him leave of absence from school for the day. —This explanation was approved by the committee.—Father Finegan denied that the matter was formally reported to or approved by the committee.— The Chairman : I think the Clerk should have consulted the committee before granting leave.—The Clerk said he considered it au emergency, and it entirely escaped his memory to report to the committee subsequently.—Father Clarke remarked that it was not the Clerk's business to em- ploy or find clerks for the returning fficer at the election. I—Father Finegan reiterated that he distinctly said the school I rsuat be kept at work as usual.—The Chairman remarked that it was an error of judgment on Mr. llanby'a part to let Mr. Hunter go without taking the chairman of the com- mittee into consultation, but he had explained that it was an . emission the he did not report the matter to the committee. Schoolmasters were servants, and undertook to do certain work. It was the returning officer's duty to find poll clerks. —Father Finegan said he did no.wish to question the pro- priety of Mr. llanby acting as presiding officer, because al- though some of the schools wereclosed others were open. It was a question that could be raised of his absenting him- self without leave.—Mr. Danbp I asked the chairmen of my committee, and he cave his sanction—Dr. O'Keeffe said as chairmen of the Finance Committee he saw no ob- jection to ME. Danhy acting as presiding officer, and he gave his sanction.--Father Finegan : That's all right.—Dr. O'Keeffe added that Mr. Allen, clerk to the Local Board, was also acting as presiding officer by the leave of Mr. Handley, chairman of the Finance Committee.—After some further conversation' Mr..Danby said there was no blame attaching to Mr. Hodter ; if there was any blame at all it attached to him.—The subject shortly afterwards dropped.

SHOCKING DEATH OF A CHILD. Hannah Harrison, three years of sge, daughter of a collier named Isaac Har- rison, rtf 26.Prospect•road, Parr, died on Monday from in- juries reeived on the previous Wednesday under shocking circumstances. On the last-named day deceased was play- ing with two ther children in a neighbouring butcher's shop, when she got a piece of a wooden skewer in her eye, making a wound about 21- inches deep. The child screamed And a womon named Eliza Mitchell pulled the wood opt. , The citiid NVNA taken home. and. her eye bathed and pouf- I tictd, but as she got worse Dr. Reid was called in. His ser- vices were, however, of no avail, and death ensued on Mon• Icy night. An inquest on the body of the deceased was held before Mr. Brighouse, coroner, on Thursday forenoon, and after hearing evidence to the foregoing effect the jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

THREATENING THE PRINCE OF WALEA—John Magee (23) and Sarah Magee (19). husband and, wife, were charged at Bow-street lam evening with having at- tempted to extort money from the Prince of Wales by menaces. The evidence given showed that the Prince of Wales had received two lettere, and in consequence an appointment was made: Two police officers attended and saw the prisoners walking about there in a suspicious manner. They were arrested separately, and then wrote a statement that the writing in the male pri- sonerie pocket book correepondesl with the w Ating in the letters sent to the Prince of Wales. Both prisoners were rerrande4. The letters stated that the writer was a member of a secret society, that he hail been told off to assassinate the Prince of Wales, and that he wanted £750 so that he could leave this country for America, and so be Mgt of treasonable conepi. acies for ever,

ANTI-VACCINATORS : A PLEA FOR TOLERATION. see from a paragraph in your last week's paper that several more of the Earlestown an'i-vaccinators have been summoned for not having had their children vaccin- ated. Now there are sot a few people who think—and I confess lam rather inclined to agree with I.l3PM—that there is something harsh and oppressive about the treat- ment of the anti vaccinator. They are convinced that this resistance to vaccination is due more to the simplicity and credulity of the people engaged in it than to any perverse desire to set the law at defiance; and, they argue, that. I simple and credulous people ought not to be punished by process of law solely because of their simplicity and credo. liry. There is another plea for tolerance in this matter which .1 think has not been urged by any of your anti-vac- cinatiodcorrespondents. It is a plea put forward by some seientiic man and is to the effect that as there is a con- tinual struggle for existence amongst men, ts amongst all other animated beings, it is desirable that the survival of the fittest should be promoted in every possible way. It is Icontended that as anti-vaccinators are for the most part simple and-credulous or obstinate and stupid people, it is not politic or in the interests of human progress to save them from the inevitable punishment of their own weakness or folly. It has been objected that it is the helpless chil- dren who will be the sufferers by a policy of this kind, but hare again the scientist takes his stand upon an inexorable natural law, that of heredity. and argues that as the chil- dren as a rile inherit the qualities and disposition of the plants the plea still beide hood. I admit that there is Something very cold-blended about arguments of this kind ; they smack it little too much of the old dispensation ways ,rryieiting the sins of the fathers on the children for iny liklne, bat tiil as anti-vaccinators have not heen very suer. tessfel in making converts of late, except amongst candi- dates before the election, they are arguments which might not be so ineffective as some they use. .
