div.head: FREE IMFORCS.7FACTS .VERSUS THEORY.
div.p: FREE IMFORCS.7FACTS .VERSUS THEORY.

Sir,—An eloquent politician said lately that "there were two methods) of philosophising— one was to form a theory, and then twist the facts to fit it ; the other was to collate the facts and draw con- clusions from a comparieen of them." The former of theee methods is the one adapted by oar " Free Trade " friends. They have a theory that a system of free imports is the best of all commercial aysterns under any conceivable set of conditions and they hold to this theory with a fana- ticism that is almost astounding in these sceptical days when the apos'olic injunction to prove all things and hold to that which is true is so generally shsers ed. A theory as we all know is a mere idle fiction, of no worth or valuelahatever if it he not based on fact, and it may not he unineirrictiye to briefly contract tide theory of the advan- tages of free imports with the facts that support it or ought to support it. The theory is tbat under the bracing in- fluence of free imports Industries thrive and grow; and th at in the artificial atmosphere of Protection they dwindle and die. The fact is that in the early part of this century, when England was protectionist, her manufacturing and commercial supremacy was so great that other nations were simply nowhere in comparison ; whilst now that England freely imports and other na- tions protect, the latter, though most of them heavily handicapped with bloated armaments ,and the consequent abstraction from productive employments of a large part of their most vigorous manhood for military pur- poses, are rapidly gaining in the industrial race and pro. muse to soon place themselves abreast of if not to distance this country. The them y is that free imports increase the well-losing of a nation and that protection decreases it. The fact is that in this country of free imports the question of bow to deal with the chronic poverty of the masses of the people is the social question of the day; while, as has hem recently attested on L'lseral platforms in this tawn, you find no such poverty in other, and protectionist countries. The theory is that people will find life easier in a country of free imports. The fact is that the chief remedy for poverty and pauperism in tbie country, advocated by sup- porters of free imports, is emigration. Emigration to where? To protectionist America and to protectionist Australia. These are the countries to which the struggling poor of Great Britain are recommended to improve their condition. Again, the theory is that free imports have been the meat's of cheapening food and the other necessaries and conveni- encas of life. The fact is that the agency which has cheapened all these thip¢s is the application of scientific discoveries to industrial purposes. If any of von i readers want proof of this let them consider the ec.ndiqon we sheuld bo in if themethods of manufacture and the Means of con- veyance wee the same as they were forty or fify years ago. when the policy of free imports was first adopted in this country. After they have done this they can scaicely to soy other conclusion thatiathat, even though univeireal free trade existed, nearly all those commodities which are now regarded as necessaries of life would be twriati, or fifty times dearer than they are at present. And, finally the theory is that the adoptioe of a policy of free imports' is a mark of the enlightenment of a nation, and the adoption of protection an indication of ignorance. nut what are tha facts that should support this theory? That Germany, the land of proferwore and students and high-class education is protectionist ; that the United S;ates. pre-eminent for intel- lectual freedom, and whose people' are least hampered by musty traditions and degmaa, are protectionist ; and that Canada and Australia, inhabited by the elite of the Anglo-Saxon race, also are protectionist; whilst outside these islands the sole practicer of any- I thing like a eystem of free imports is the Turk—the "unspeakable " and illiterate Turk. Surely one must come to the conclusion that a theory was never so badly supported by facts as this theory of free imports. TO THE LIBERAL ELECTORS OF KNCTS- FORD DIVISION OF CHESHIRE. GENTLIMSN,—After an exceptionally arduous contest it is my pleasing duty to thank you most heartily for the support I and assistance which you have so freely rendered to the Liberal cause and to my candidature. My best thanks are due to many of the new electors who worked so hard on my behalf, and also to all those who oc- cupied any official position in the Division, for the time and sacrifices which they made. Although the issue was not such as I and our party wished for, yet I believe that with the spread of political Information Liberalism will, upon some future occasion, if its adherents continue to display the same amount of determination and perseverance in the future as they have done in the post, gain the victory in the consti- tuency. Thanking you further for the personal kindness and con- sideration which I have uniformly received at your bands, I have the honour to be, Gentlemen, Tour obedient servant, EMMOTT BARLOW. I Torkington Lodge, near Stockport. Dec. 14th, 1885.
